Whole-course orientation

Build the bacterial differential from the outside in

This is the map for all seven lectures. The actual lesson starts in Tab 2. Follow the same order for every organism: shape/stain → oxygen/growth → rapid lab branch → virulence → clinical syndrome → specimen/test → lecture treatment and prevention.

7 lecture sources
1

Shape & stain

Cocci, rods, curved rods, spirochetes, branching filaments, or acid-fast bacilli.

2

Oxygen

Aerobic, facultative, microaerophilic, anaerobic, or obligately intracellular.

3

Fast test

Catalase, coagulase, hemolysis, oxidase, lactose, urease, H₂S, motility.

4

Virulence

Capsule, toxin, adhesin, intracellular survival, enzyme, pigment, or biofilm.

5

Correct specimen, transport, medium, stain, antigen/antibody test, NAAT, culture.

6

Control

Lecture-listed drugs, source control, isolation, sanitation, vaccination, contacts.

Lesson 1.07

Aerobic Cocci

Begin with the branching tests, then connect each structure and toxin to the syndrome it produces. This tab follows the lecture through Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Neisseria, clinical disease, diagnostic markers, resistance, treatment, and prevention.

Aerobic Cocci pp. 1–14
Learning-objective map
  • Describe the nature, classification, and distinguishing characteristics of cocci.
  • Recognize the lecture’s disease burden, distribution, and patient predilection.
  • Correlate pathogenesis and immune response with clinical manifestations and emergencies.
  • Match diagnostic markers with the correct examination and culture method.
  • Identify lecture-listed treatment and resistance mechanisms.
  • Explain infection control, prophylaxis, and immunization where included.

First branching decisions

QuestionPositive branchNegative or alternate branch
Catalase?Staphylococcus forms bubbles because catalase converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.Streptococcus and Enterococcus show no bubbling.
Coagulase?S. aureus converts fibrinogen to fibrin and produces visible clumping.S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are coagulase negative.
Novobiocin?S. epidermidis is sensitive.S. saprophyticus is resistant.
Alpha hemolysis?S. pneumoniae is optochin sensitive and bile soluble.Viridans streptococci are optochin resistant and bile insoluble.
Beta hemolysis?S. pyogenes is bacitracin sensitive and PYR positive.S. agalactiae is bacitracin resistant, CAMP positive, and hippurate positive.
Neisseria carbohydrate use?N. gonorrhoeae uses glucose only.N. meningitidis uses glucose and maltose.

Staphylococci

Staphylococcus aureus pp. 1–4 and appendix

Identity and morphology

  • Gram-positive cocci classically arranged in clusters that resemble grapes.
  • May also appear singly, in pairs, tetrads, or short chains.
  • Young cultures stain strongly Gram positive. Older cultures may appear less strongly Gram positive.
  • Golden-yellow colonies on blood agar.
  • Facultative anaerobe, nonmotile, and non-spore-forming.
  • Normal skin and nasal flora in about one-fourth of the population in the lecture.
  • Disease follows overgrowth, high bacterial load, skin damage, direct invasion, toxin production, or a combination.

Catalase, coagulase, and specimens

  • Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide and produces visible bubbling.
  • Extracellular coagulase converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin.
  • Fibrin produces visible clumping and helps separate S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci.
  • Specimens include surface swabs, pus or abscess aspirate, blood, endotracheal aspirate, sputum, and CSF.
  • Nasal swabs are used when assessing colonization.
  • Gram-positive clusters alone do not distinguish S. aureus from other staphylococci. Culture and biochemical testing are required.

Structural virulence factors

  • Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG and interferes with opsonization.
  • Polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis.
  • Coagulase forms a fibrin coat around the organism.
  • Hyaluronidase digests hyaluronic acid and supports spread through tissue.
  • Staphylokinase dissolves fibrin clots and releases bacteria.
  • Teichoic acids contribute to cell-wall metabolism.
  • Peptidoglycan stimulates IL-1 release, complement activation, PMN attraction, and opsonic antibody production.

Biofilm and dissemination

  • Biofilm forms on IV catheters, prosthetic valves, and artificial joints.
  • The extracellular polysaccharide matrix reduces antibiotic penetration.
  • Cells divide more slowly within biofilm.
  • Bacteria can exchange genetic material and resistance genes within the community.
  • Bloodstream spread may reach muscle, bone, joints, heart valves, lungs, brain, and epidural space.
  • Vegetations can embolize and seed distant organs.

Toxins and their consequences

ToxinMechanism in the lectureClinical result
TSST-1Acts as a superantigen by linking MHC class II and T-cell receptors, causing a cytokine storm.Toxic shock syndrome with abrupt fever, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgia, scarlatiniform or sunburn-like rash, hypotension, and possible cardiac or renal failure.
Panton-Valentine leukocidinPhage-encoded pore-forming toxin that lyses leukocytes and releases inflammatory mediators.Severe inflammation, tissue necrosis, and destructive pneumonia or skin disease.
Alpha hemolysinTargets eukaryotic cell membranes.Cell injury and hemolysis.
Beta hemolysinDegrades sphingomyelin.RBC toxicity.
Delta hemolysinDisrupts cell membranes.Linked in the lecture to diarrheal disease.
Gamma hemolysin or leukocidinLyses white blood cells.Inflammation and tissue destruction.
Exfoliative toxins A and BDissolve the mucopolysaccharide matrix of the epidermis.Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome or Ritter disease with generalized desquamation.
EnterotoxinsHeat-stable and resistant to gut enzymes.Food poisoning after 1 to 8 hours with violent nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Fever is usually absent and recovery is rapid.

Localized and skin disease

  • Progression may begin with a pimple or folliculitis.
  • A furuncle is a boil.
  • A carbuncle is a cluster of furuncles.
  • Impetigo affects the epidermis.
  • Cellulitis reaches the dermis and spreads across the skin.
  • A subcutaneous abscess is a walled-off pocket of pus and may contain septations.
  • Abscesses may also occur in the mouth, liver, kidney, spleen, or brain.

Disseminated disease

  • Muscle infection causes pyomyositis.
  • Bone infection causes osteomyelitis.
  • Joint infection causes septic arthritis.
  • Infected blood clot causes septic thrombophlebitis.
  • Bacteremia can trigger vasodilation, hypotension, poor organ perfusion, and sepsis.
  • Endocarditis produces vegetations with embolic spread.
  • Severe pneumonia, meningitis, and epidural abscess may follow hematogenous spread.

Resistance mechanisms

  • Plasmids commonly carry resistance to tetracyclines, erythromycins, and aminoglycosides.
  • Beta-lactamase destroys the beta-lactam ring of many penicillins.
  • Beta-lactamase inhibitors such as clavulanic acid block selected beta-lactamases.
  • Methicillin resistance is independent of beta-lactamase.
  • mecA encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein that beta-lactams cannot effectively bind.
  • SCCmec types distinguish hospital-associated and community-associated MRSA in the lecture.
  • VISA has intermediate vancomycin resistance. VRSA has complete resistance.

Treatment and control

  • Clinically important isolates require antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
  • Closed suppurative lesions require drainage.
  • Local antiseptic care helps prevent recurrent abscesses.
  • The lecture lists clindamycin and vancomycin as common MRSA choices.
  • Alternatives listed include tetracyclines, TMP-SMX, linezolid, tigecycline, daptomycin, and quinupristin-dalfopristin.
  • Hospital control uses surveillance, hand hygiene, and strict contact precautions.
  • High-risk areas include nurseries, ICUs, operating rooms, and chemotherapy wards.
If you seeGram-positive clusters, catalase positivity, coagulase positivity, purulent infection, rapid toxin syndrome, or destructive endocarditis point to S. aureus.

Staphylococcus epidermidis

  • Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
  • Catalase positive and coagulase negative.
  • Novobiocin sensitive.
  • Normal skin and nasal or throat flora.
  • Main virulence factor is biofilm.
  • Associated with prostheses, shunts, intravascular catheters, prosthetic valves, and artificial joints.
  • Risk is increased in very young, older, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Persistent device infection may require device removal in addition to antimicrobial therapy.

Exam cue: coagulase-negative staphylococcus plus an implanted device.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus

  • Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
  • Catalase positive and coagulase negative.
  • Novobiocin resistant.
  • Classic lecture association is UTI in young women.
  • Differentiate from S. epidermidis through novobiocin testing and the urinary clinical context.

Exam cue: young woman with UTI and novobiocin resistance.

Streptococci

Classification frame
  • Gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains.
  • Catalase negative.
  • Facultative anaerobes.
  • Classified by hemolysis, Lancefield carbohydrate antigen, biochemical reactions, physical resistance, ecology, and clinical syndrome.
HemolysisAppearance on blood agarMajor lecture organisms
AlphaPartial hemolysis with green discoloration.S. pneumoniae and viridans streptococci.
BetaComplete clearing around colonies.S. pyogenes and S. agalactiae.
GammaNo visible hemolysis.Nonhemolytic streptococcal groups in the lecture classification chart.
Streptococcus pneumoniae pp. 5–6

Identity and laboratory

  • Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci.
  • Alpha hemolytic.
  • Optochin sensitive.
  • Bile soluble.
  • Encapsulated.
  • Found in the nasopharynx.
  • Capsule can be demonstrated by Quellung reaction.

Virulence and immune relevance

  • Polysaccharide capsule is the major antiphagocytic structure.
  • Capsule is especially important in evading alveolar macrophages.
  • The spleen clears opsonized encapsulated bacteria.
  • Asplenic patients are at risk of overwhelming postsplenectomy infection.
  • IgA protease breaks down mucosal IgA and permits respiratory mucosal invasion.

Clinical syndromes

  • MOPS means meningitis, otitis media, pneumonia, and sinusitis.
  • Pneumonia may produce fever, cough, pleuritic pain, and rust-colored sputum in the lecture.
  • Otitis is emphasized in children.
  • Meningitis is especially concerning in asplenia, extremes of age, and impaired immunity.

Diagnosis, treatment, prevention

  • Gram stain may show lancet diplococci.
  • Alpha hemolysis plus optochin sensitivity and bile solubility differentiates it from viridans streptococci.
  • Quellung demonstrates capsular swelling.
  • The lecture lists penicillin, macrolides, and third-generation cephalosporins according to context.
  • Vaccination and protection of high-risk asplenic patients are important preventive themes.
Streptococcus viridans group pp. 6–7

Identity

  • Umbrella group that includes S. mutans, S. mitis, and S. sanguinis in the lecture.
  • Gram positive and catalase negative.
  • Alpha hemolytic.
  • Optochin resistant.
  • Bile insoluble.
  • Usually nonencapsulated.
  • Normal oropharyngeal flora.

Virulence and disease

  • Biofilm supports oral adhesion and dental plaque.
  • S. mutans and S. mitis are linked to oral biofilm and gingival or dental disease.
  • Dextrans bind to fibrin-platelet aggregates on damaged heart valves.
  • S. sanguinis is the lecture cue for bloodstream spread and endocarditis.
  • Subacute endocarditis develops on pre-existing abnormal or prosthetic valves.

Diagnosis and prevention

  • Differentiate from pneumococcus by optochin resistance and bile insolubility.
  • Clinical context includes dental disease, recent oral bloodstream entry, and abnormal valves.
  • The lecture lists amoxicillin prophylaxis in selected patients at high risk of subacute endocarditis.
Lecture cues
  • Mute or mutans means mouth for oral disease.
  • Sanguine means blood for S. sanguinis and endocarditis.
Streptococcus pyogenes or Group A Streptococcus pp. 7–8

Identity

  • Gram-positive cocci in chains.
  • Catalase negative.
  • Beta hemolytic.
  • Bacitracin sensitive.
  • Lancefield Group A.
  • PYR positive.
  • Nasopharyngeal association supports pharyngitis.

Virulence factors

  • M protein is antiphagocytic and supports adherence.
  • Hyaluronic-acid capsule resembles host tissue and resists phagocytosis.
  • Streptolysin O is oxygen labile and antigenic.
  • Streptolysin S is oxygen stable and contributes surface hemolysis.
  • Streptokinase dissolves fibrin.
  • DNases break down DNA in pus.
  • Hyaluronidase supports tissue spread.
  • Pyrogenic exotoxins produce scarlet fever and toxic shock patterns.

Clinical disease

  • Pharyngitis and tonsillitis.
  • Impetigo and skin infection.
  • Erysipelas and cellulitis.
  • Rapid invasive soft-tissue infection and necrotizing disease.
  • Scarlet fever with toxin-mediated rash.
  • Streptococcal toxic shock with systemic instability.

Immune sequelae

  • Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngeal infection only in the lecture.
  • Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow pharyngeal or skin infection.
  • These are immune-mediated rather than direct bacterial invasion of the affected organ.

Diagnosis and treatment

  • Use throat or lesion specimens according to syndrome.
  • Beta hemolysis, bacitracin sensitivity, PYR positivity, and Group A antigen support identification.
  • Antistreptolysin O may support evidence of prior infection.
  • The lecture’s management centers on appropriate beta-lactam therapy and prompt treatment of pharyngitis.

Prevention

  • Early diagnosis and treatment limit transmission and selected immune sequelae.
  • Use respiratory and contact precautions according to the clinical setting.
  • Recognize invasive soft-tissue disease and toxic shock as emergencies.
Streptococcus agalactiae or Group B Streptococcus p. 8

Identity

  • Gram-positive cocci in chains.
  • Catalase negative.
  • Beta hemolytic.
  • Bacitracin resistant.
  • Lancefield Group B.
  • PYR negative.
  • Hippurate positive.
  • CAMP positive.
  • Colonizes the female genital tract and lower gastrointestinal tract.

Clinical disease and risk groups

  • Maternal vaginal colonization may transmit infection during delivery.
  • Neonates may develop sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis.
  • Older adults and immunocompromised patients may develop invasive disease.
  • Lecture risk factors include diabetes, cancer, advanced age, liver cirrhosis, corticosteroid use, HIV, and other immunocompromised states.
  • Adult manifestations include bacteremia, skin or soft-tissue infection, respiratory infection, and genitourinary infection.

Diagnosis and prevention

  • Use maternal screening and organism identification through beta hemolysis, CAMP, hippurate, and Group B antigen.
  • The lecture emphasizes intrapartum prophylaxis for colonized or high-risk patients.
  • Rapid identification in the newborn is important because invasive disease can progress quickly.

Gram-negative diplococci

FeatureN. gonorrhoeaeN. meningitidis
CapsuleAbsent.Polysaccharide capsule present.
Carbohydrate useGlucose only.Glucose and maltose.
Main portalGenital, rectal, pharyngeal, or conjunctival mucosa.Nasopharynx.
Main spreadSexual contact and perinatal exposure.Respiratory droplets and hematogenous spread.
Main emergencyPID, infertility, disseminated gonococcal infection, neonatal eye disease.Meningitis, meningococcemia, DIC, shock, and adrenal hemorrhage.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae pp. 8–10

Identity and laboratory

  • Gram-negative kidney-shaped diplococci.
  • Oxidase positive.
  • Often seen intracellularly in neutrophils.
  • Uses glucose but not maltose.
  • No polysaccharide capsule.
  • Culture can use Thayer-Martin selective medium.
  • NAAT identifies bacterial genetic material and is a major diagnostic anchor.

Virulence

  • Pili attach to epithelial cells and resist mechanical washing by mucus, urine, and vaginal secretions.
  • Pili undergo antigenic and phase variation.
  • Variation contributes to repeated infection and lack of durable immunity.
  • Opa proteins support close attachment.
  • Por proteins regulate membrane transport and host interaction.
  • IgA protease supports mucosal survival.
  • Lipooligosaccharide produces endotoxin-related inflammation.

Clinical syndromes

  • Urethritis with purulent discharge and dysuria.
  • Cervicitis that may be asymptomatic.
  • Ascending infection may cause PID, infertility, or ectopic-pregnancy risk.
  • Rectal and pharyngeal infection may occur.
  • Disseminated infection may produce dermatitis, tenosynovitis, and septic arthritis.
  • Newborn exposure may cause ophthalmia neonatorum.

Treatment and prevention

  • The lecture lists ceftriaxone as first-line treatment.
  • Chlamydial treatment is added when coinfection is possible or not excluded.
  • Evaluate and treat sexual partners.
  • Prevention includes reducing sexual partners, early detection, screening high-risk groups, condoms, and contact tracing.
  • Newborn ocular prophylaxis is listed with erythromycin or tetracycline ophthalmic ointment.
Neisseria meningitidis pp. 10–11

Identity and diagnosis

  • Gram-negative diplococci.
  • Oxidase positive.
  • Uses glucose and maltose.
  • Specimens include blood, CSF, petechial aspirate, and nasopharyngeal swab.
  • Gram stain may show intracellular or extracellular diplococci.
  • Culture on chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin.
  • Latex agglutination or molecular tests may detect capsular antigen or bacterial targets.

Virulence and susceptibility

  • Pili attach to nasopharyngeal epithelium and undergo antigenic variation.
  • IgA protease supports mucosal survival.
  • LOS lipid A triggers severe systemic inflammation.
  • Polysaccharide capsule prevents phagocytosis.
  • Capsule incorporates human sialic-acid derivatives and produces molecular mimicry.
  • Asplenia and sickle-cell disease increase vulnerability to encapsulated organisms.
  • Terminal complement deficiency from C5 to C9 increases susceptibility.

Pathogenesis and meningitis

  • Humans are the only natural host.
  • Organism enters through the nasopharynx.
  • Pili support attachment and IgA protease supports persistence.
  • Bacteremia permits hematogenous spread.
  • Crossing the blood-CSF barrier produces meningeal inflammation.
  • Symptoms include fever, severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, phonophobia, and rapid progression to coma.

Meningococcemia emergency

  • LOS release causes massive inflammation and capillary leakage.
  • Coagulation activation produces DIC and thrombocytopenia.
  • Petechial or hemorrhagic rash appears on the trunk and extremities.
  • Capillary leakage produces hypovolemic shock.
  • Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome results from adrenal hemorrhage, ischemia, necrosis, and acute adrenal insufficiency.

Treatment and prevention

  • The lecture lists ceftriaxone for treatment.
  • Rifampin is listed for prophylaxis of close contacts.
  • Vaccination targets capsular serogroups included in the lecture.
  • Rapid treatment, droplet precautions, and contact prophylaxis are essential.
Do not missFever, meningismus, petechiae or purpura, hypotension, and DIC indicate meningococcemia and require immediate action.
Lesson 1.09

Gram-Positive Rods

This tab keeps the lecture’s Gram-positive rods together. The curved Gram-negative rods that appeared later in the same lecture remain in the Gram-Negative Non-Enterics tab. Each organism below includes morphology, culture, virulence, host interaction, clinical disease, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

Gram-Positive Rods pp. 1–8
Learning-objective map
  • Recognize morphological, cultural, and structural characteristics.
  • Relate virulence factors to pathogenicity and host-microbe interaction.
  • Enumerate clinical manifestations and important complications.
  • Identify the correct specimen, culture method, and confirmatory test.
  • Match lecture-listed drugs and prevention measures with organism properties.

Sporulation and germination

Form or processConditionLecture meaning
Vegetative cellFavorable nutrients, moisture, and temperatureActively growing form. Bacilli in living animals and humans are generally vegetative rather than sporulated.
SporulationLow nutrients, low moisture, dead tissue, soil, or other unfavorable conditionsThe organism produces a dormant endospore containing genetic material within several protective protein coats.
EndosporeEnvironmental survivalExtremely resistant to heat, drying, chemicals, and other physical conditions. Spores may remain viable for years.
GerminationMoist, nutrient-rich surface at the proper temperatureThe spore returns to a vegetative cell and resumes growth.
InactivationAutoclavingThe lecture states that spores are inactivated at 120°C for 15 minutes.
Culture-age clue
  • A 24-hour Bacillus culture may not yet show spores.
  • A 72-hour culture is more likely to demonstrate spores because nutrients have become depleted.
  • The lecture describes the spore as oval, centrally located, and not distending the cell in B. anthracis.

Bacillus species

FeatureB. anthracisB. cereus
Main exposureAnimal products, contaminated food, or inhaled spores.Ingestion of contaminated food or traumatic soil-contaminated eye injury.
MotilityNonmotile.Motile in the lecture comparison.
Main virulenceD-glutamate capsule and PA, EF, LF exotoxins.Enterotoxins and glycoprotein S-layer.
Culture clueMedusa-head colony and gamma-phage lysis.Not lysed by gamma phage in the lecture comparison.
High-yield diseaseMalignant pustule, Woolsorter disease, and gastrointestinal anthrax.Emetic or diarrheal food poisoning and ophthalmic infection.
Bacillus anthracis pp. 1–2

Morphology and ecology

  • Large straight Gram-positive rods with right-angle or boxcar-like ends.
  • May appear singly, in pairs, or in short chains.
  • Central oval spores do not distend the cell.
  • Spores are found in older cultures, soil, and dead animals.
  • Primary hosts are herbivores.
  • Humans are accidental hosts.

Transmission

  • Skin contact with contaminated hides, wool, hair, or animal tissue can cause cutaneous anthrax.
  • Ingestion of contaminated food can cause gastrointestinal anthrax.
  • Inhalation of contaminated dust can cause Woolsorter disease.
  • Herbivores ingest contaminated vegetation or inhale spores from soil or water.

Capsule

  • Made of D-glutamic acid rather than polysaccharide.
  • Antigenic and antiphagocytic.
  • Produced in infected animals and humans.
  • Encoded by plasmid pXO2.
  • Loss of the capsule reduces virulence.

Exotoxin components

  • Encoded by plasmid pXO1.
  • Heat labile.
  • Protective antigen supports attachment and entry of the toxin components.
  • Edema factor raises intracellular cAMP and inhibits neutrophil phagocytosis.
  • Lethal factor promotes macrophage death through the inflammatory pathways described in the lecture.
  • The three components act together to produce systemic anthrax.

Host-microbe interaction

  • Macrophages attempt to engulf the bacilli.
  • Capsule and exotoxin make destruction difficult.
  • Macrophages release IL-1, TNF, and oxygen radicals.
  • Toxin-mediated macrophage injury supports systemic spread and severe inflammation.

Clinical manifestations

  • Cutaneous anthrax begins after spores enter a wound.
  • The lesion becomes a painless dark pustule or black eschar.
  • A ring of vesicles and marked edema may surround the eschar.
  • Facial or neck edema may occur.
  • The eschar may enlarge while the surrounding vesicles and edema diminish.
  • Pulmonary anthrax produces hemorrhagic mediastinal lymph-node disease, respiratory distress, and cyanosis.
  • The lecture warns that untreated pulmonary disease may lead to death within 24 hours.
  • The organism is listed as a Category A biological weapon.

Laboratory diagnosis

  • Use material from a malignant pustule, sputum for pulmonary disease, or blood for septicemia.
  • Bicarbonate agar demonstrates capsule production through a mucoid colony.
  • Blood agar shows the irregular fringe-like Medusa-head colony.
  • Gamma phage lysis supports B. anthracis. Lack of lysis points toward B. cereus in the lecture.
  • Mouse inoculation is described historically but is limited by animal-testing concerns.
  • ELISA detects antibodies.

Treatment and prevention

  • The lecture lists ciprofloxacin or doxycycline with one or two additional antibiotics for severe disease.
  • Additional drugs listed include rifampin, vancomycin, penicillin, and imipenem.
  • Dead animals should be buried deeply to prevent pasture contamination.
  • Animal products from outbreak areas should be sterilized.
  • Animals receive a live-spore vaccine using the Sterne strain.
  • The lecture describes a killed-spore vaccine for humans during control efforts.
If you seePainless black eschar after animal-product exposure or inhalational illness with massive mediastinal widening points to anthrax.
Bacillus cereus pp. 2–3

Food and spore cycle

  • Also called Chinese Restaurant Syndrome in the lecture.
  • Common food associations include cereals, fried rice, milk, pasta, meat, and contaminated sauces.
  • Vegetative cells in cooked or uncooked rice may lyse.
  • Released endospores survive steaming and rapid frying.
  • After ingestion, spores germinate into vegetative cells.
  • Vegetative cells produce enterotoxin and cause gastroenteritis.

Virulence factors

  • Enterotoxin is the major cause of gastrointestinal disease.
  • The lecture notes peptidoglycan, teichoic acid, and cytoplasmic membrane as cell-wall features.
  • Glycoprotein S-layer supports attachment and interaction with polymorphonuclear cells.
FormToxinIncubationFood cluePattern
EmeticHeat-stable enterotoxin.1 to 6 hours.Fried rice, milk, and pasta.Staphylococcal-like rapid vomiting syndrome.
DiarrhealHeat-labile enterotoxin.6 to 24 hours.Meat and sauces.Cholera-like watery diarrheal syndrome.

Ophthalmic disease

  • May cause severe inflammation after penetrating eye trauma.
  • Soil-contaminated objects are an important exposure.
  • The lecture lists vancomycin, clindamycin, and gentamicin for this setting.

Management and prevention

  • Food poisoning is described as self-limiting in the lecture comparison.
  • Prevention depends on proper cooking, storage, reheating, and food handling.
  • Do not rely on rapid frying alone to eliminate heat-resistant spores.
Mnemonic“Be serious” when thinking of fried rice and Bacillus cereus.

Bacillus thuringiensis

  • Used as a larvicide.
  • Produces a protein lethal to selected insect larvae.
  • The lecture emphasizes Diptera such as flies and mosquitoes.
  • Protein production is associated with DNA and plasmids.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae pp. 3–4

Morphology

  • Gram-positive bacillus with swelling at one or both ends.
  • Swelling contains metachromatic granules.
  • Granules are also called Babes-Ernst, volutin, or inorganic-phosphate granules.
  • Snapping division produces X, Y, V, and Chinese-letter arrangements.
  • Biotypes listed are gravis, intermedius, and mitis.
  • Each biotype may be toxigenic or nontoxigenic.

Toxin genetics and structure

  • Exotoxin production is a lysogenic property.
  • Beta prophage carries the tox gene.
  • Without the prophage, the organism is nontoxigenic.
  • Subunit B binds to the host-cell surface and permits entry.
  • Subunit A carries ADP-ribosylation activity.

Toxin mechanism

  1. Subunit B binds the host membrane.
  2. Subunits A and B enter through receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  3. Subunit A separates after cleavage.
  4. Subunit A interrupts transfer of the growing polypeptide chain.
  5. ADP-ribosylation inactivates elongation factor 2.
  6. Protein synthesis stops and host cells die.

Clinical manifestations

  • Cutaneous disease follows puncture wounds and may occur with toxigenic or nontoxigenic strains.
  • Cutaneous lesions may form deep erosive nonhealing ulcers with gray-brown membrane.
  • Respiratory colonization involves the tonsils, nose, and throat.
  • Host-cell death produces a greenish-gray pseudomembrane.
  • Cervical lymph-node swelling produces a bull-neck appearance.
  • Complications include airway obstruction, myocarditis, cranial-nerve paralysis, and muscle paralysis.

Laboratory diagnosis

  • Collect a nasopharyngeal or throat swab.
  • Loeffler slant enhances demonstration of volutin granules.
  • Potassium tellurite produces gray-black colonies.
  • The lecture describes black colonies on blood agar.
  • Elek toxigenicity test uses antitoxin-impregnated filter paper and precipitation lines.
  • Include positive control, negative control, and test organism.

Treatment and prevention

  • Antitoxin prevents further binding of toxin fragment B.
  • Penicillin is listed as an antibiotic adjunct to antitoxin.
  • Antitoxin neutralizes circulating toxin but does not reverse toxin already inside cells.
  • Humans are the only reservoir in the lecture.
  • Prevention uses diphtheria toxoid and Tdap vaccination.
  • Exposed contacts receive prophylaxis and close surveillance.
ABCDE(F)G
  • A means ADP-ribosylation.
  • B means beta prophage.
  • C means Corynebacterium.
  • D means diphtheriae.
  • E means elongation factor.
  • G means granules.
Listeria monocytogenes pp. 4–6

Exposure and risk groups

  • Found in soil, water, animals, meat, poultry, seafood, raw milk, and food-processing environments.
  • High-risk foods include sprouts, unpasteurized milk, soft cheese, cold deli meats, hot dogs that are not reheated, and smoked seafood.
  • Severe disease is emphasized in pregnant patients, newborns, older adults, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Serotype 4b is linked to foodborne outbreaks.

Laboratory characteristics

  • Short Gram-positive rods that may resemble streptococci when in short chains.
  • Facultative intracellular organism.
  • Produces acid but not gas from carbohydrates.
  • Motile with tumbling motility at 25°C but not at 37°C.
  • Catalase positive.
  • Esculin hydrolysis positive.
  • Produces a narrow beta-hemolytic zone on 5% sheep blood agar.
  • Tolerates 2°C to 4°C, low pH, and high-salt conditions.
  • The lecture explicitly lists “endotoxin” as a characteristic. It is retained here as a lecture-specific statement.

Virulence factors

  • D-galactose residues support adherence to host receptors.
  • Internalin A and B mediate zipper-like entry into host cells.
  • Listeriolysin O perforates the phagosomal membrane.
  • Phospholipase C A helps escape the first vacuole.
  • ActA recruits host actin at one pole and drives intracellular movement.
  • Phospholipase C B helps escape the double-membrane vacuole after cell-to-cell spread.
  • Catalase and superoxide dismutase neutralize oxidative killing.
  • Iron is noted as an important virulence factor.

Intracellular life cycle

  1. Internalin A and B permit entry.
  2. LLO and PlcA lyse the first vacuole.
  3. The organism replicates in the cytoplasm.
  4. ActA produces polarized actin polymerization.
  5. Actin propels the bacterium to the host-cell membrane.
  6. A listeriapod enters the neighboring cell.
  7. LLO and PlcB lyse the double membrane.
  8. The cycle repeats without prolonged extracellular exposure to antibodies or complement.

Pathogenesis and clinical disease

  • Ingested organisms enter the gut and spread to lymph nodes and blood.
  • Bloodstream spread reaches the liver, spleen, brain, and placenta.
  • Pregnancy disease may cause septicemia, placental abscess, and spontaneous abortion.
  • Early neonatal disease may present as granulomatosis infantiseptica.
  • Late neonatal disease commonly presents as meningitis.
  • Children, neonates, older adults, and immunocompromised patients may develop meningitis or meningoencephalitis.
  • Bacteremia and focal infection may occur.

Diagnosis, treatment, prevention

  • Use tumbling motility, narrow beta hemolysis, catalase positivity, culture, and clinical exposure.
  • The lecture notes a CSF pattern of high PMNs, low glucose, and normal protein.
  • Drugs listed include ampicillin, vancomycin, and ciprofloxacin.
  • Pregnant and immunocompromised patients should avoid unpasteurized milk products and raw vegetables in the lecture prevention section.
  • High-risk foods should be heated and handled safely.

Minor Gram-positive rods and branching organisms

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae p. 6

Ecology and identity

  • Animal pathogen found especially in swine, fish, and other animal products.
  • Fishermen, butchers, and animal handlers are high-risk groups.
  • Resistant to smoking, pickling, and desiccation.
  • Catalase negative, oxidase negative, and indole negative.

Virulence and disease

  • Hyaluronidase breaks down hyaluronic acid in connective tissue.
  • Neuraminidase cleaves N-acetylneuraminic acid and supports adhesion.
  • Human disease is called erysipeloid.
  • Seal finger or whale finger follows direct contact with infected fish or meat through traumatized skin.
  • The lesion is painful, swollen, and slowly spreading.
  • Do not confuse erysipeloid with erysipelas caused by Group A Streptococcus.

Diagnosis and control

  • Collect aspirate or biopsy from the active edge of the lesion.
  • Culture on blood agar under the lecture conditions.
  • Penicillin is the lecture treatment.
  • Use protective equipment when handling infected animal tissue.
  • Animals may receive a live attenuated vaccine.
Lactobacilli p. 6

Normal-flora role

  • Found in the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and vagina.
  • Use available sugars or glycogen for energy.
  • Produce lactic acid as a by-product.
  • Acid production helps maintain an acidic environment.

Laboratory and practical use

  • Gram-positive non-spore-forming rods.
  • Nonmotile.
  • Facultative anaerobes that tolerate very little oxygen.
  • Grow on MRS agar as small white creamy colonies.
  • Used as probiotics in sour milk, cheese, yogurt, and commercial preparations.
  • Used in fermented vegetables, beverages, sourdough, and selected sausages.
Streptomyces pp. 6–7

Characteristics and environmental role

  • Gram-positive aerobic filamentous bacteria.
  • Form chains of spores at maturity.
  • Produce red, pink, brown, gray, and other colorful fungal-like colonies.
  • Decompose organic matter in soil.
  • Contribute to the earthy odor of soil and decaying leaves.
  • Support soil fertility.

Products and clinical disease

  • S. venezuelae is listed for chloramphenicol and daptomycin production.
  • S. griseus produces streptomycin.
  • S. rimosus and S. aureofaciens produce tetracyclines.
  • S. fradiae produces neomycin.
  • S. lincolnensis produces lincomycin.
  • S. avermitilis produces ivermectin.
  • S. sudanensis and S. somaliensis cause mycetoma.
  • Mycetoma may produce hard or black granules in wounds.

Diagnosis

  • Direct microscopy shows Gram-positive filamentous rods.
  • Culture shows colorful colonies.
  • Histopathology demonstrates bacillary granules.
  • PCR may support identification.
Nocardia p. 7

Ecology and morphology

  • Ubiquitous saprophyte found in soil, water, and organic matter.
  • The lecture also notes healthy gingiva as a possible normal-flora site.
  • Gram-positive branching filamentous rod.
  • Weakly acid-fast and stains light pink.
  • Less intensely acid-fast than Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Transmission and disease

  • Inhalation can produce pulmonary infection.
  • Dissemination may reach the brain and kidney.
  • Traumatic implantation may produce mycetoma.
  • N. brasiliensis is the lecture species associated with mycetoma.
  • Immunocompromised patients are particularly vulnerable to invasive disease.

Diagnosis

  • Use sputum, blood, tissue, or granule specimens according to the syndrome.
  • Direct microscopy shows branching Gram-positive weakly acid-fast filaments.
  • Histopathology may show grains surrounded by neutrophils.
  • PCR supports species identification.
  • BCYE culture may produce breadcrumb colonies after 2 to 10 days in the lecture.
Do not confuse
  • Nocardia is aerobic and weakly acid-fast.
  • Actinomyces is anaerobic, non-acid-fast, and linked to sulfur granules.
  • Streptomyces is an aerobic soil organism known for colorful colonies and antibiotic production.
Lesson 1.08

Gram-Negative Enterics

This tab follows the lecture from the shared Enterobacteriaceae framework to the six major organisms. Each organism is organized by structure, colony appearance, biochemical reactions, virulence, host response, clinical disease, complications, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

Enterobacteriaceae pp. 1–15
Learning-objective map
  • Describe the nature, characteristics, and classification of the enteric bacilli.
  • Recognize the lecture’s Philippine distribution, morbidity, mortality, and high-risk groups.
  • Connect microbiologic pathogenesis and host response with clinical manifestations.
  • Recognize complications and emergencies such as septic shock, intestinal perforation, and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
  • Correlate colony color, biochemical markers, antigenic structures, and molecular targets with the correct diagnostic test.
  • Identify the lecture-listed treatment, resistance patterns, prevention, and patient education measures.

Enterobacteriaceae framework

GroupOrganismsLecture meaning
Opportunistic pathogensEscherichia, Klebsiella, Proteus, CitrobacterThey may belong to normal gut flora. They become pathogenic when they move outside their usual habitat, acquire pathogenic traits, or infect a vulnerable host.
True pathogensSalmonella, ShigellaThey are presented as organisms that directly cause disease rather than merely acting after displacement from normal flora.
Shared laboratory featureMeaning
Gram-negative rodsThey stain pink to red because of the thin peptidoglycan layer and safranin counterstain.
Catalase positiveThey can break down hydrogen peroxide.
Oxidase negativeThis separates most enterics from oxidase-positive non-enteric rods such as Pseudomonas.
Nitrate positiveThe lecture includes nitrate reduction as a shared physiologic property.
Glucose fermentersTSI reactions then distinguish lactose or sucrose use, gas, and hydrogen sulfide production.

Antigenic structures

AntigenLocation and functionImportant lecture exceptions
O antigen
Somatic
  • Outermost repeating sugar portion of lipopolysaccharide.
  • Heat-stable.
  • Contributes to endotoxin-associated inflammation and immune evasion.
  • All Enterobacteriaceae in the lecture have an O antigen.
Used to classify strains and serogroups.
H antigen
Flagellar
  • Protein component of flagella.
  • Heat-labile.
  • Produces a strong immune response.
  • Reflects motility.
Absent in Shigella and Klebsiella.
K antigen
Capsular
  • Acidic polysaccharide capsule.
  • Heat-labile.
  • Prevents phagocytosis.
  • Called the Vi antigen in Salmonella Typhi.
Absent in Shigella and Proteus.
F antigen
Fimbrial
  • Protein hair-like appendages.
  • Support attachment to urinary or intestinal epithelium.
  • May support conjugation and transfer of resistance genes.
Important in UPEC, Klebsiella, Proteus, and Citrobacter pathogenesis.
Lecturer mnemonics
  • FaKSHet means Klebsiella and Shigella have no flagellar H antigen.
  • K(e)SH P means Shigella and Proteus have no K antigen.
  • “Kawawa ako lang walang exotoxin” is the lecture cue that Klebsiella is listed as the only Enterobacteriaceae without exotoxin.

Colony colors and biochemical identification

OrganismColony appearanceTSI and major reactionsFast differentiator
Escherichia coli
  • Blood agar: large, circular, gray, moist colonies.
  • MacConkey: pink to red.
  • EMB: metallic green sheen.
  • SMAC: usual strains turn pink. O157:H7 remains colorless or pale.
  • TSI A/A with gas.
  • No H₂S.
  • IMViC positive, positive, negative, negative.
  • Indole positive.
  • Motile.
  • Urease negative.
Rapid lactose fermentation plus metallic green EMB sheen.
Salmonella
  • MacConkey: colorless.
  • SS: colorless with black centers.
  • HE: blue-green with black centers.
  • XLD: red with black centers.
  • TSI K/A with gas and H₂S.
  • Indole negative.
  • Urease negative.
  • Motile.
  • Vi capsule in Typhi.
Motile non-lactose fermenter with H₂S production.
Shigella
  • MacConkey: colorless.
  • SS: colorless without black centers.
  • HE: green or blue-green.
  • XLD: red or pink translucent colonies.
  • S. sonnei may ferment lactose slowly.
  • TSI K/A.
  • No gas.
  • No H₂S.
  • Nonmotile.
  • Urease negative.
No H antigen, no K antigen, and no motility.
Klebsiella
  • MacConkey: large bright pink to red, wet, mucoid colonies.
  • Blood agar: large gray wet mucoid colonies.
  • EMB: large pink to purple mucoid colonies without metallic sheen.
  • CLED: large yellow mucoid colonies.
  • TSI A/A with heavy gas.
  • No H₂S.
  • IMViC commonly negative, negative, positive, positive in the lecture.
  • Urease positive.
  • Nonmotile.
Thick capsule, mucoid colonies, and positive string test in hypermucoviscous strains.
Proteus
  • MacConkey: pale or colorless.
  • Blood or nutrient agar: swarming wave-like film.
  • SS and XLD: colonies may have black centers.
  • CLED: isolated blue-green colonies because swarming is suppressed.
  • TSI K/A with heavy H₂S.
  • Strong urease positive.
  • Phenylalanine deaminase positive with a deep green reaction.
  • MR positive.
  • VP negative.
  • Citrate positive.
  • P. vulgaris is indole positive.
Swarming plus intense urease activity.
Citrobacter
  • MacConkey: pale to pink.
  • XLD: yellow with black center.
  • HE: yellow-orange.
  • EMB: dark purple to black.
  • Standard media may produce earthy-brown or amber colonies.
  • TSI is usually A/A with variable H₂S.
  • MR positive.
  • VP negative.
  • Citrate positive.
  • Usually motile.
  • Indole and urease vary by species.
May resemble E. coli or Salmonella. Use TSI, LIA, citrate, motility, and species identification.
Lecture comparison notes
  • Citrobacter is placed with lactose fermenters, although some species produce H₂S.
  • Shigella sonnei can be a slow lactose fermenter.
  • Serratia is usually taught as a non-lactose fermenter, although some strains ferment lactose late. S. marcescens may produce red prodigiosin pigment.
  • Yersinia is nonmotile at 37°C. Y. enterocolitica is usually urease positive.
  • Providencia urease results vary by species.
Escherichia coli pp. 1–3 and appendix

Medical importance and epidemiology

  • Beneficial normal gut flora and major pathogen.
  • Leading lecture cause of community-acquired and hospital-acquired UTI.
  • Also associated with sepsis, pneumonia, neonatal meningitis, foodborne gastroenteritis, and HUS.
  • Diarrheal disease is underreported and rises during rainy seasons and contaminated-water outbreaks.
  • The lecture lists children younger than 5, adults older than 60, patients with chronic disease, catheter users, and communities with poor WASH infrastructure as high-risk groups.
  • The lecture reports 75% of UTI and more than 20% of bacteremia in tertiary hospitals.

Structure and laboratory identity

  • Short straight Gram-negative rods that may appear singly or in random groupings.
  • Outer membrane contains LPS and acts as a permeability barrier and endotoxin source.
  • Periplasm contains thin peptidoglycan and enzymes for transport and antibiotic degradation.
  • Peritrichous flagella provide motility.
  • Fimbriae support adherence. Sex pili transfer plasmids by conjugation.
  • Plasmids may carry toxin and antibiotic-resistance genes.
  • 70S ribosomes are targets of several antibiotic classes.

Virulence and pathogenesis

  • UPEC P fimbriae bind kidney and urinary epithelial cells against urinary flushing.
  • Intimin anchors EPEC and EHEC to the intestinal wall.
  • Type III secretion injects bacterial proteins that reorganize actin and create attaching-and-effacing lesions.
  • A/E lesions destroy microvilli and reduce water absorption.
  • LPS and O antigen can trigger hypotension and septic shock during bacteremia.
  • LT and ST enterotoxins drive water and electrolyte secretion in ETEC.
  • Stx1 and Stx2 inhibit protein production in EHEC and can cause colonic hemorrhage and kidney injury.

Host response

  • Mechanical flushing produces intestinal hypermotility and urinary frequency.
  • TLR4 recognizes LPS and activates TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6.
  • Cytokine-driven vasodilation produces inflammation, swelling, and fever.
  • Neutrophils phagocytose bacteria. Dead neutrophils and bacteria produce pyuria.
  • Adaptive antibodies target O, H, and K antigens.
  • Antibodies neutralize toxins, block flagellar movement, and opsonize capsulated bacteria.

Diarrheagenic and extraintestinal types

TypeMain mechanism in the lectureClinical patternDiagnostic target
ETEC
Enterotoxigenic
  • Colonization-factor fimbriae.
  • Heat-labile LT toxin.
  • Heat-stable ST toxin.
Traveler’s watery diarrhea with cramps, nausea, vomiting, low fever, and dehydration.PCR for lt and st genes.
EPEC
Enteropathogenic
  • Intimin and Type III secretion.
  • Attaching-and-effacing lesion.
  • Extracellular attachment rather than Shigella-like intracellular invasion.
Severe infantile or pediatric watery diarrhea.PCR for the eae intimin gene.
EHEC or STEC
Enterohemorrhagic or Shiga-toxin producing
  • A/E attachment.
  • Stx1 and Stx2 inhibit protein synthesis.
  • O157:H7 is the lecture prototype.
Severe cramps with watery diarrhea that becomes bloody. High fever is usually absent. HUS may appear after apparent improvement.
  • SMAC shows colorless or pale O157:H7 colonies.
  • ELISA detects Shiga toxin.
  • PCR detects stx1 and stx2.
EIEC
Enteroinvasive		Appendix describes a Shigella-like invasive pattern.Watery diarrhea that may progress to dysentery.Differentiate from Shigella through organism identification and the broader biochemical pattern.
EAEC
Enteroaggregative
  • Aggregative fimbriae.
  • Biofilm formation.
  • Plasmid-encoded heat-stable enterotoxin variant in the appendix.
Mucoid diarrhea.Molecular and pathotype-specific identification when available.
UPEC
Uropathogenic
  • P and Type 1 fimbrial attachment.
  • Ascending urinary infection.
Cystitis, pyelonephritis, urosepsis, dysuria, urgency, frequency, cloudy or foul-smelling urine, and possible hematuria.Midstream urine, urinalysis, culture, nitrite, and leukocyte esterase.

Other clinical manifestations

  • Urosepsis and bacteremia may follow untreated urinary or abdominal infection.
  • Sepsis may produce fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, hypoperfusion, and multiorgan failure.
  • Neonatal meningitis is associated with protective capsulated strains, particularly in premature newborns.
  • Newborn findings include poor feeding, irritability, high-pitched crying, lethargy, and bulging fontanelle.

HUS emergency

  • The lecture states that 5% to 10% of STEC infections develop HUS.
  • It commonly appears 5 to 10 days after diarrhea when the patient seems to be improving.
  • Hemolytic anemia produces fatigue and pallor.
  • Thrombocytopenia produces petechiae and low platelets.
  • Acute kidney failure produces oliguria or anuria and edema.

Diagnosis

  • Use urine for UTI, stool for diarrhea, and blood cultures for sepsis.
  • Gram stain shows short Gram-negative rods.
  • MacConkey is bright pink. EMB has a metallic green sheen.
  • IMViC is positive, positive, negative, negative.
  • TSI is A/A with gas and no H₂S.
  • Latex agglutination detects specific O or H antigens.
  • VITEK, MicroScan, MALDI-TOF, ELISA, and PCR are included in the lecture.

Treatment and prevention

  • Mild to moderate diarrhea receives oral rehydration solution.
  • Severe dehydration may require IV Lactated Ringer’s solution.
  • Do not use loperamide when EHEC is suspected.
  • The lecture restricts antibiotics in EHEC or STEC because bacterial stress may increase HUS risk.
  • Uncomplicated UTI agents listed include nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, and TMP-SMX.
  • Complicated UTI or pyelonephritis agents listed include ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin.
  • ESBL sepsis options listed include carbapenems or piperacillin-tazobactam.
  • Prevention emphasizes handwashing, food cooking, avoiding cross-contamination, produce washing, safe water, chlorination, and antimicrobial stewardship.
Salmonella pp. 3–5 and appendix

Classification and structure

  • Medically divided into nontyphoidal Salmonella and typhoidal Salmonella.
  • Gram-negative motile rods with peritrichous flagella.
  • O antigen varies among serotypes.
  • H antigen can undergo phase variation between two flagellin types.
  • Vi capsular antigen protects S. Typhi and selected Paratyphi strains from immune recognition.
  • Fimbriae promote attachment to intestinal M cells.

Culture and biochemical profile

  • Non-lactose fermenter with colorless MacConkey colonies.
  • SS agar produces colorless colonies with black centers.
  • HE agar produces blue-green colonies with black centers.
  • XLD agar produces red colonies with black centers.
  • TSI is K/A with gas and H₂S.
  • Motile, indole negative, and urease negative.

Pathogenesis

  • Invades intestinal M cells using Type III secretion.
  • Induces membrane ruffling and internalization.
  • Survives inside Salmonella-containing vacuoles.
  • Nontyphoidal strains produce local neutrophilic inflammation and tissue injury.
  • Typhoidal strains survive in macrophages and spread through the bloodstream.
  • LPS contributes to systemic inflammatory responses.

Host response

  • TLR4 recognizes LPS and TLR5 recognizes flagellin.
  • Caspase-1 activation drives pyroptosis and IL-1β and IL-18 release.
  • Neutrophils damage the infected gut lining during gastroenteritis.
  • Th1 cells produce IFN-γ to activate infected macrophages.
  • B cells produce antibodies against O and H antigens.
Clinical formManifestationsComplications
Nontyphoidal gastroenteritis
  • Foodborne illness.
  • Fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and watery or bloody diarrhea.
  • Inflammation is driven by intestinal invasion and neutrophilic tissue damage.
Dehydration and bacteremia in vulnerable patients.
Typhoid or enteric fever
  • Prolonged step-ladder fever.
  • Relative bradycardia or Faget sign.
  • Rose spots.
  • Constipation or abdominal symptoms.
  • Altered mental status or typhoid state in severe disease.
  • Intestinal bleeding.
  • Intestinal perforation.
  • Sepsis and systemic spread.
  • Chronic gallbladder carriage.

Diagnosis

  • Use stool for gastroenteritis.
  • Use blood cultures early in typhoid disease.
  • Urine, stool, and bone marrow may be used later or in selected settings.
  • Selenite F or tetrathionate broth enriches recovery.
  • Serotype with O, H, and Vi antigens.
  • Slide agglutination, PCR, MALDI-TOF, and automated systems are included.
  • The lecture discusses the Widal test as a serologic method.

Treatment and prevention

  • Fluid replacement is central in gastroenteritis.
  • Antibiotic treatment is guided by syndrome, severity, and susceptibility.
  • Typhoid treatment must account for resistance.
  • Prevention emphasizes safe food, clean water, proper cooking, sanitation, carrier control, and vaccination for typhoid where indicated.
If you seeMotility, H₂S, black-centered colonies, and systemic enteric fever clues point to Salmonella. The Vi capsule specifically supports S. Typhi.
Shigella pp. 5–7 and appendix

Classification and identity

  • True human pathogen that causes shigellosis or bacillary dysentery.
  • Very low infectious dose and high person-to-person transmissibility.
  • Four O-antigen serogroups.
  • Group A is S. dysenteriae.
  • Group B is S. flexneri.
  • Group C is S. boydii.
  • Group D is S. sonnei.
  • No H antigen and no K antigen.

Laboratory pattern

  • Nonmotile and usually non-lactose fermenting.
  • S. sonnei may ferment lactose slowly.
  • MacConkey and SS colonies are colorless.
  • No black center because H₂S is absent.
  • TSI is K/A without gas and without H₂S.
  • Indole varies by species.
  • MR positive, VP negative, citrate negative, and urease negative.

Virulence and invasion

  • Invasion plasmid antigens or Ipa proteins drive epithelial invasion.
  • Type III secretion delivers effectors into host cells.
  • After vacuolar escape, the organism multiplies in the cytoplasm.
  • IcsA or VirG produces a polar actin tail.
  • Actin-based movement permits cell-to-cell lateral spread without extracellular exposure.
  • S. dysenteriae produces Shiga toxin that inhibits protein synthesis and can cause HUS.

Host response and clinical disease

  • Pyroptosis and cytokine release recruit neutrophils.
  • Neutrophil migration damages the colonic mucosa.
  • Early watery diarrhea may progress to frequent small-volume stools.
  • Classic stool contains blood, mucus, and pus.
  • Fever, abdominal cramps, and tenesmus are characteristic.
  • Severe disease may produce toxic megacolon, bacteremia, seizures in children, or HUS.

Diagnosis

  • Collect fresh stool containing blood, mucus, or pus.
  • Use Cary-Blair transport medium when transport is delayed.
  • Culture on MacConkey, SS, HE, and XLD.
  • Serogroup with A, B, C, and D antisera.
  • PCR detects the ipaH gene.
  • ELISA or PCR can detect Shiga toxin.

Treatment and prevention

  • Replace fluids and electrolytes.
  • Use the lecture-listed antimicrobial therapy when indicated and guided by local resistance.
  • Avoid antidiarrheal drugs in invasive or Shiga-toxin disease.
  • Prevention emphasizes hand hygiene, isolation precautions, disinfection, safe food and water, and fly control.
Bloody-diarrhea distinction
  • Shigella commonly produces fever, tenesmus, blood, mucus, and pus.
  • EHEC commonly produces severe cramps and bloody diarrhea without high fever, followed by possible HUS.
  • Salmonella is motile and H₂S positive. It may cause inflammatory diarrhea or systemic enteric fever.
Klebsiella pneumoniae pp. 7–8 and appendix

Identity and antigenic structure

  • Short plump Gram-negative rods with a very thick polysaccharide capsule.
  • Nonmotile because the organism lacks H antigen.
  • O antigen is located beneath the capsule and contributes endotoxin activity.
  • K antigen forms the antiphagocytic capsule.
  • Type 1 and Type 3 fimbriae attach to host tissue and medical devices.
  • Siderophores such as enterobactin and yersiniabactin acquire iron.
  • The lecture lists no exotoxin for Klebsiella.

Culture and biochemistry

  • Rapid lactose fermenter with large bright pink mucoid MacConkey colonies.
  • Blood agar colonies are large, gray, wet, dome-shaped, and nonhemolytic.
  • EMB colonies are pink to purple and mucoid without metallic sheen.
  • TSI is A/A with gas and no H₂S.
  • IMViC is commonly negative, negative, positive, positive in the lecture.
  • Urease is weakly to moderately positive.
  • Motility is negative.

Pathogenesis and host response

  • Capsule prevents phagocytosis and interferes with complement.
  • Fimbriae support urinary and respiratory colonization.
  • Type 3 fimbriae support biofilm on catheters and ventilator tubing.
  • Siderophores support rapid replication in tissue.
  • TLR4 detection of LPS triggers TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6.
  • Neutrophil extracellular traps attempt to contain bacteria.
  • Neutrophil enzymes also cause alveolar necrosis, bleeding, and thick mucus.
  • Capsule-specific antibodies support opsonization.

Clinical manifestations

  • Necrotizing lobar pneumonia in chronic alcohol use, diabetes, immunocompromise, or ventilated patients.
  • Sudden fever, chills, productive cough, pleurisy, dyspnea, cyanosis, and currant-jelly sputum.
  • Chest imaging may show abscesses and cavitation.
  • Community-acquired and hospital-acquired UTI, especially with catheters.
  • Sepsis, bacteremia, neonatal meningitis, and pyogenic abscesses.
  • Hypervirulent strains can produce liver abscess with metastatic endophthalmitis or meningitis in previously healthy people.

Diagnosis and resistance

  • Use sputum, urine, blood, or CSF according to syndrome.
  • India ink or capsule methods may visualize the capsule.
  • String test longer than 5 mm supports hypermucoviscosity.
  • Use susceptibility testing because ESBL and carbapenemase production are major concerns.
  • PCR targets listed include blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48, and blaVIM.

Treatment and prevention

  • Lecture-listed susceptible-strain options include ceftriaxone, piperacillin-tazobactam, or levofloxacin.
  • ESBL strains are treated with carbapenems in the lecture.
  • CRE options listed include ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, polymyxins, or tigecycline.
  • Supportive care may include oxygen and ventilation.
  • Prevent through hand hygiene, contact isolation, dedicated equipment, environmental cleaning, catheter minimization, ventilator protocols, comorbidity control, and antimicrobial stewardship.
Proteus pp. 8–10 and appendix

Identity and structure

  • Opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen associated with complicated UTI and stone formation.
  • P. mirabilis and P. vulgaris are the main lecture species.
  • Peritrichous flagella permit extreme motility and swarming.
  • MR/P and PMF fimbriae attach to urinary epithelium and catheters.
  • Plasmids may carry multidrug-resistance and beta-lactamase genes.
  • Proteus lacks the K capsular antigen in the lecture.

Urease and stone mechanism

  • Urease converts urea into ammonia.
  • Ammonia raises urinary pH and produces alkaline urine with an ammonia odor.
  • Alkaline urine precipitates magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate.
  • This produces struvite stones and may form staghorn calculi.
  • Stones and crystalline biofilm protect bacteria from immune clearance and antibiotics.
  • Stones irritate the urinary tract and may cause hematuria and obstruction.

Culture and biochemistry

  • Non-lactose fermenter with pale or colorless MacConkey colonies.
  • Swarming on blood and nutrient agar produces concentric waves.
  • TSI is K/A with heavy H₂S and blackening.
  • Urease is rapidly and intensely positive with a bright fuchsia reaction.
  • Phenylalanine deaminase is positive with a deep green slant.
  • Gelatin liquefaction is positive.
  • P. vulgaris is indole positive. P. mirabilis is commonly indole negative in the lecture tree.

Clinical and host response

  • Catheter-associated UTI, cystitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia, and wound infection.
  • TLR4 recognition of LPS triggers IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α.
  • IL-8 recruits neutrophils and contributes pyuria.
  • Stones create persistent inflammation, tissue injury, obstruction, and recurrent infection.
  • Antibodies may target flagella and urease, although stones remain a major immune-evasion structure.

Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention

  • Use urine, wound swab, or blood according to syndrome.
  • Confirm with urease, TSI, PAD, swarming, automated identification, or MALDI-TOF.
  • The Weil-Felix test uses Proteus OX strains as cross-reacting antigens for selected rickettsial antibodies. It is not a test for Proteus infection itself.
  • Lecture-listed oral choices include ampicillin, cephalexin, or ciprofloxacin.
  • ESBL options listed include carbapenems or piperacillin-tazobactam.
  • Remove stones when necessary through PCNL or ESWL.
  • Acetohydroxamic acid is listed as a urease inhibitor for chronic unresectable stones.
  • Prevent through catheter stewardship, closed drainage, hydration, urine acidification measures, hand hygiene, and contact precautions.
Citrobacter pp. 10–12 and appendix

Medical importance and structure

  • Opportunistic Enterobacteriaceae and emerging healthcare-associated pathogen.
  • Some C. freundii isolates have a capsule that mimics the Vi antigen of S. Typhi.
  • LPS lipid A contributes endotoxin and septic shock.
  • The periplasm may contain AmpC beta-lactamase.
  • Fimbriae support attachment to bladder, intestinal, and brain-capillary endothelium.
  • Most strains are motile through peritrichous flagella.
  • Plasmids and transposons may carry ESBL or carbapenemase genes such as NDM-1.

Culture and biochemistry

  • MacConkey colonies range from pale to pink.
  • XLD may show yellow colonies with black centers.
  • HE may show yellow-orange colonies.
  • EMB may show dark purple to black colonies.
  • Lactose, H₂S, indole, and urease vary by species.
  • MR is positive, VP is negative, and citrate is positive.
  • Most strains are motile.

Pathogenesis

  • Some strains use a LEE-encoded Type III secretion system to form attaching-and-effacing lesions.
  • A/E lesions destroy microvilli and produce watery diarrhea.
  • Selected C. freundii strains may acquire Shiga toxin and produce bloody diarrhea or kidney injury.
  • C. koseri uses outer-membrane proteins to cross the blood-brain barrier.
  • Biofilm supports urinary and device-associated infection.
  • LPS may produce sepsis.

Clinical manifestations

  • Gastroenteritis and diarrhea.
  • UTI and pyelonephritis.
  • Sepsis and bacteremia.
  • Intra-abdominal and wound infection.
  • Neonatal meningitis and brain abscess, particularly with C. koseri.

Diagnosis and resistance

  • Use urine, blood, wound specimens, or CSF.
  • Differentiate from E. coli and Salmonella with TSI, LIA, citrate, motility, and species identification.
  • Use VITEK, MALDI-TOF, PCR, AmpC testing, and ESBL testing when needed.
  • Species-level identification matters because reactions vary.

Treatment and prevention

  • Choose therapy through susceptibility testing because AmpC, ESBL, and carbapenemase resistance may occur.
  • Supportive treatment is required for diarrhea and sepsis.
  • Prevention emphasizes hand hygiene, device care, infection-control precautions, and antimicrobial stewardship.

Complete gastroenteritis comparison from the appendix

Organism or pathotypeAttachment or invasionMajor toxin or intracellular featureLecture disease
SalmonellaInvades M cells through Type III secretion.Pyroptosis and Salmonella-containing vacuoles.Nontyphoidal gastroenteritis or systemic typhoidal disease.
ShigellaType III secretion and Ipa-mediated invasion.IcsA actin tail, lateral intracellular spread, and Shiga toxin in S. dysenteriae.Shigellosis, dysentery, and HUS.
EHECAttaching-and-effacing lesion.Stx1 and Stx2.Hemorrhagic colitis and HUS.
EIECShigella-like invasion.Intracellular invasive pattern.Watery diarrhea and dysentery.
EPECAttaching-and-effacing lesion while remaining extracellular.Intimin and Type III secretion.Severe infantile diarrhea.
ETECColonization-factor fimbriae.Heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins.Traveler’s watery diarrhea.
EAECAggregative fimbriae and biofilm.Plasmid-encoded heat-stable enterotoxin variant in the lecture appendix.Mucoid diarrhea.
End-of-tab decision rule
  • Pink or red MacConkey means lactose fermentation. Think first of E. coli or Klebsiella.
  • Metallic green EMB strongly points to E. coli.
  • Large mucoid pink colonies point to capsulated Klebsiella.
  • Black centers point to H₂S producers such as Salmonella, Proteus, or selected Citrobacter.
  • Nonmotile without H₂S points to Shigella.
  • Swarming and urease point to Proteus.
Lesson 1.10 and curved rods from Lesson 1.09

Gram-Negative Non-Enterics and Curved Rods

This tab keeps the organisms in the lecture sequence while expanding the clues used for identification. Focus on oxygen use, lactose fermentation, oxidase reaction, pigment, odor, growth temperature, required growth factors, environmental reservoir, animal exposure, and specialized media.

Non-Enteric pp. 1–10 · GP Rods pp. 8–11
Learning-objective map
  • Give the morphological, cultural, and structural characteristics of the organisms.
  • Describe the virulence factors and connect each factor with pathogenicity.
  • Explain the host-microbe interaction, including biofilm formation and intracellular survival.
  • Enumerate the clinical manifestations and recognize the characteristic exposure clues.
  • Match the organism with the correct specimen, culture medium, biochemical test, serology, or molecular test.
  • Identify the lecture-listed antimicrobial treatment and prevention measures.
  • Differentiate non-enteric rods from enteric rods by fermentation, oxidase reaction, environmental habitat, and clinical syndrome.

How to approach the group

First clueWhat it suggestsOrganisms emphasized in the lecture
Oxidase-positive non-lactose fermenterThink of a non-enteric environmental rod rather than Enterobacteriaceae.Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia pseudomallei
Blue-green pigment, fluorescence, fruity odor, growth at 42°CA single cluster of laboratory clues strongly supports Pseudomonas.P. aeruginosa
Small fastidious coccobacillus that needs blood-derived factorsAsk whether X factor, V factor, chocolate agar, or satellitism is present.Haemophilus influenzae
Water aerosol and intracellular growth in macrophagesThink of a fastidious organism from cooling towers, hot-water systems, or similar reservoirs.Legionella pneumophila
Bipolar or safety-pin stainingUse the exposure and disease pattern to separate the organisms.Burkholderia pseudomallei, Pasteurella multocida, Yersinia pestis
Curved, comma, gull-wing, or vibrio-shaped rodUse microaerophilic growth, urease, marine exposure, and special media.Campylobacter, Helicobacter, Vibrio
Pseudomonas aeruginosa Non-Enteric pp. 1–3

Identity and habitat

  • Gram-negative rod and an opportunistic pathogen.
  • May be part of normal skin flora.
  • Can cause disease after reaching a site outside its usual habitat or after host barriers are injured.
  • Requires only a minimal amount of nutrients.
  • May contaminate contact-lens solutions, faucet openings, moist hospital surfaces, respiratory equipment, hot tubs, and spas.
  • Can grow at a maximum temperature of 42°C.
  • Has a single polar flagellum in the free-swimming form.

Two basic forms

  • Free-swimming form consists of individual motile cells.
  • Biofilm form consists of a community of bacteria held in the slime layer.
  • Free cells multiply and organize into a biofilm.
  • The biofilm matures and later breaks down.
  • Breakdown releases new free-swimming cells that can spread to other sites.
  • The slime layer is loosely attached and differs from a tightly organized capsule.

Why the biofilm matters

  • Supports attachment to host surfaces and respiratory tissue.
  • Weakens respiratory ciliary function.
  • Creates a barrier that reduces antibiotic penetration.
  • Protects the organisms from phagocytosis.
  • Explains persistence in cystic fibrosis, respiratory devices, catheters, and other chronically contaminated surfaces.
  • Contributes to the difficulty of eradicating the organism even after antimicrobial therapy is started.

Type IV pili and flagellum

  • Type IV pili are important for attachment.
  • The lecture notes that attachment commonly requires prior host-cell injury.
  • Examples include damaged nasal mucosa and an open burn wound.
  • The single polar flagellum supports motility and helps the organism reach a favorable surface.
  • Pili also participate in genetic exchange and are connected with the R-factor drug-resistance plasmid in the lecture.

Virulence factors and their effects

Virulence factorLecture-supported actionClinical connection
Lipopolysaccharide
  • Acts as endotoxin.
  • Triggers fever, shock, oliguria, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Severe bacteremia and systemic inflammatory disease.
Exotoxin A
  • Blocks protein synthesis.
  • Presented as antiphagocytic in the lecture.
Tissue injury and invasive infection.
Exoenzyme S
  • Acts as an adhesin to glycolipids on respiratory cells.
  • Produced in burned tissue.
Respiratory attachment and burn-associated disease.
Phospholipase CAttacks pulmonary cells and produces atelectasis and necrosis.Destructive pneumonia.
Alkaline protease
  • Breaks down fibrin.
  • Associated with hemorrhagic skin lesions and corneal infection.
Skin and eye disease.
Elastase
  • Breaks down elastic fibers in alveolar walls.
  • Interferes with ciliary function.
  • Degrades IgG, IgA, complement, collagen, and coagulation factors.
Chronic lung damage and impaired local immune defense.
Pyocyanin
  • Blue-green water-soluble pigment.
  • Damages other microbes and supports nutrient acquisition in the lecture.
Blue-green colony or discharge clue.
PyoverdinYellow-green fluorescent pigment.Fluorescence under ultraviolet light.
PyochelinRed-brown siderophore that obtains iron when environmental iron is low.Supports survival and multiplication in the host.

Predisposing factors

  • Respiratory equipment.
  • Cystic fibrosis.
  • Contaminated syringes or needles among drug users.
  • Immunocompromised state.
  • Severe burns and other injuries.
  • Catheters and invasive instruments.
  • Contact-lens contamination.

Clinical manifestations

  • Burn and wound infection.
  • Pneumonia, including device-associated and cystic-fibrosis disease.
  • Conjunctivitis and corneal infection.
  • Endocarditis.
  • Bone and joint infection.
  • Urinary tract infection after catheters, instruments, or contaminated irrigation solution.
  • Meningitis or brain abscess after spread from the inner ear, paranasal sinuses, or invasive procedures.

Characteristic syndromes

  • External otitis or swimmer’s ear with greenish discharge after contaminated water exposure and maceration.
  • Ecthyma gangrenosum in bacteremia, including the neonatal burn case shown in the lecture.
  • Hot-tub folliculitis after inadequately chlorinated pools, spas, or whirlpools.
  • Green nail syndrome.
  • Corneal infection after contact-lens contamination.

Laboratory diagnosis and resistance

  • Blood agar may be used for culture.
  • MacConkey agar shows a non-lactose-fermenting colony.
  • Isolation agar demonstrates blue-green pyocyanin.
  • The culture may have a characteristic fruity odor.
  • The organism grows at 37°C and remains able to grow at 42°C.
  • The oxidase test is positive.
  • Tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine is converted into indophenols in a positive oxidase reaction.
  • Culture fluoresces under ultraviolet light because of fluorescent pigment.
  • Biofilm formation reduces antimicrobial penetration.
  • The R-factor plasmid can encode resistance to more than one antimicrobial drug.
  • The lecture lists penicillin, kanamycin, and tetracycline among resistant agents.
  • The lecture lists the aminoglycosides amikacin, gentamicin, and tobramycin among sensitive agents.
  • Prevention depends on hand hygiene, contact precautions, cleaning of equipment, and control of persistent moist reservoirs.

If you see this cluster

Oxidase-positive non-lactose fermenter + fruity odor + blue-green pigment + fluorescence + growth at 42°C strongly points to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Burkholderia species

SpeciesCharacteristics and habitatMain diseaseDiagnosis, treatment, and prevention
Burkholderia pseudomallei
  • Gram-negative obligately aerobic rod.
  • Motile, oxidase positive, and indole negative.
  • Non-lactose fermenter.
  • Can grow at 42°C.
  • Shows bipolar thickening with Wright stain.
  • Found in soil and water.
  • Classified as a Category B bioterrorism agent in the lecture.
  • Melioidosis.
  • May be recovered from blood, sputum, urine, throat swab, or aspirated pus.
  • Blood agar after 24 hours may show smooth creamy-white colonies.
  • After 48 to 72 hours, colonies become dry and wrinkled with a possible purplish hue.
  • MacConkey remains non-lactose fermenting.
  • The lecture lists ceftazidime, imipenem, meropenem, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, and TMP-SMX.
  • Common resistance includes penicillin, ampicillin, first- and second-generation cephalosporins, gentamicin, and tobramycin.
Burkholderia cepacia
  • Environmental organism in soil and water.
  • Hospital-acquired organism that frequently colonizes intravenous fluids and irrigation solutions.
  • Often resistant to commonly used antimicrobial drugs.
  • Not usually dangerous for healthy people, but important in vulnerable hosts.
  • Respiratory infection in patients with cystic fibrosis.
  • Hospital-associated infection from contaminated fluids.
  • Blood agar and nutrient agar may be used.
  • The lecture lists TMP-SMX plus ceftazidime as first-line treatment.
  • Use contact and droplet precautions.
  • Visitors and staff should clean their hands.
  • Staff should use gowns, gloves, and masks.
  • The lecture advises a two-meter separation from the patient.
Burkholderia mallei
  • Gram-negative aerobic rod.
  • Unlike the other two Burkholderia species in the lecture, it is nonmotile.
  • Does not persist in the environment.
Glanders, described as a highly communicable disease affecting livestock.API 20NE and PCR are listed for laboratory identification.
Acinetobacter baumannii Non-Enteric pp. 4–5

Ecology and transmission

  • Ubiquitous in animals, soil, and freshwater.
  • Can colonize the skin.
  • Can be recovered in high numbers from respiratory and oropharyngeal secretions.
  • Important in immunocompromised patients and in patients hospitalized for prolonged periods.
  • Sources include a colonized patient, contaminated equipment, healthcare workers’ hands, and ventilator machines.
  • Can survive desiccation and remain in the environment for several days.

Structure and virulence

  • Gram-negative coccobacillus that may appear in pairs and resemble cocci.
  • Encapsulated.
  • Capsular polysaccharide protects against phagocytosis, desiccation, host defenses, and disinfectants.
  • Contains lipopolysaccharide.
  • Outer membrane, phospholipase, biofilm, and fimbriae support survival and infection.
  • The lecture identifies antimicrobial resistance as a major determinant of clinical outcome.

Clinical manifestations

  • Ventilator-associated pneumonia.
  • Bloodstream infection.
  • Urinary tract infection.
  • Hospital-acquired pneumonia.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia.
  • Endocarditis.
  • Meningitis.
  • Skin, soft-tissue, and bone infection.

Laboratory and control

  • Oxidase negative.
  • Catalase positive.
  • Can grow at 44°C.
  • The lecture describes it as colored on MacConkey and as a lactose fermenter.
  • Grows on sheep blood agar.
  • API 20 and PCR are listed for identification and separation from A. lwoffii.
  • Clean the environment, use contact precautions, and perform hand hygiene.
  • Place MDR cases in contact isolation.
Lecture-specific treatment note
  • The lecture lists carbapenems, polymyxins, and aminoglycosides.
  • It also notes that some isolates have been reported resistant to colistin and polymyxin B.
ESKAPE mnemonic
  • E means Enterococcus faecium.
  • S means Staphylococcus aureus.
  • K means Klebsiella pneumoniae.
  • A means Acinetobacter baumannii.
  • P means Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  • E means Enterobacter species.
Haemophilus influenzae Non-Enteric pp. 5–6

Identity

  • Small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus.
  • May appear as short rods, longer rods, or rounded coccobacilli.
  • Facultative anaerobe.
  • Oxidase positive and catalase positive.
  • May show more intense staining at the poles, producing a safety-pin appearance.
  • Also called Pfeiffer’s bacillus.
  • The name Haemophilus means blood-loving.

Colonization and capsule

  • Approximately 90% of healthy individuals are described as carrying the organism as part of respiratory flora.
  • Only a small proportion of strains are encapsulated.
  • Encapsulated strains are linked with more severe invasive disease.
  • The lecture lists capsular types a through g.
  • Type b is emphasized as the major human disease-associated encapsulated type.
  • The type b capsule is made of polyribitol phosphate or PRP.

Growth requirements

  • Fastidious and unable to grow on ordinary culture media.
  • Requires X factor, which is hemin.
  • Requires V factor, which is NAD.
  • Chocolate agar releases X and V factors through heating and red-cell lysis.
  • On blood agar, S. aureus releases the factors needed by H. influenzae.
  • Small colonies grow around the S. aureus streak. This is the satellite phenomenon.

Virulence

  • Lipopolysaccharide contributes to inflammation.
  • Fimbriae paralyze ciliated respiratory epithelium and participate in otitis-media inflammation.
  • The PRP capsule inhibits phagocytosis.
  • IgA protease hydrolyzes human IgA and supports immune evasion at mucosal surfaces.

Pathogenesis and disease

Local respiratory disease

  • Colonizes the nasopharynx.
  • May cause otitis media.
  • May cause upper and lower respiratory infection.
  • May cause pneumonia.

Invasive spread

  • May enter the bloodstream.
  • Can reach the central nervous system and cause meningitis.
  • Can reach the heart and cause pericarditis.
  • Can produce cellulitis and other invasive infections.

Airway emergency

  • Epiglottitis may produce airway obstruction.
  • The lecture warns that severe obstruction may lead to suffocation.
  • Unvaccinated children are emphasized as an important risk group for Hib meningitis and invasive disease.
HEMOP mnemonic
  • H means Haemophilus.
  • E means epiglottitis.
  • M means meningitis.
  • O means otitis media.
  • P means pericarditis.

Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention

  • Choose the specimen according to the site. The lecture lists nasopharyngeal swab, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and pus.
  • Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli.
  • Culture uses chocolate agar and the satellite phenomenon on blood agar.
  • A commercial kit may detect Hib antigen in cerebrospinal fluid.
  • The lecture lists ampicillin and third-generation cephalosporins for treatment.
  • Prevention uses the DPT-Hib vaccine containing the type b PRP capsular antigen.

If you see this cluster

Small Gram-negative coccobacillus + X and V factors + chocolate agar or satellitism + epiglottitis or meningitis points to H. influenzae.

Bordetella pertussis Non-Enteric pp. 6–7

Identity and transmission

  • Small Gram-negative aerobic coccobacillus.
  • Nutritionally fastidious and needs a rich blood-containing medium.
  • Young cultures may be capsulated and older cultures may lose the capsule.
  • Humans are the only known reservoir.
  • Transmitted by droplets during close contact.
  • The lecture notes that large droplets travel short distances and do not remain suspended.

Adhesion factors

  • Filamentous hemagglutinin supports adherence.
  • Pertactin supports adherence.
  • Attachment to respiratory epithelium allows colonization and prevents removal.

Toxins

  • Adenylate-cyclase toxin reduces phagocytic activity and causes red-cell hemolysis.
  • Lethal or dermonecrotic toxin causes inflammation.
  • Pertussis toxin contributes to colonization and the toxemic stage.
  • Tracheal cytotoxin damages ciliated cells, stimulates IL-1 release and fever, and inhibits DNA synthesis.

Laboratory diagnosis

  • A nasopharyngeal specimen may be plated onto charcoal agar.
  • Blood agar or Bordet-Gengou agar is listed.
  • Selective antibiotics may suppress competing organisms.
  • The organism may be recovered during the first three weeks.
  • Culture may require prolonged incubation.
  • PCR, direct immunofluorescence, and ELISA are listed.

Clinical course

1

Incubation
Usually less than three weeks. FHA and pertactin support colonization, followed by toxin release.

2

Catarrhal stage
Weeks 0 to 2. Mild cough, sneezing, and runny nose. This is the highly contagious period.

3

Ciliary injury
