Toxins paralyze and damage the respiratory cilia. Secretions become difficult to clear.

4

Paroxysmal stage
Weeks 2 to 8. Repeated uncontrolled coughing, excessive secretions, bronchiolar obstruction, and a high-pitched inspiratory whoop.

5

Tissue response
Necrosis and polymorphonuclear infiltration may accompany the severe coughing stage.

6

Convalescent stage
Weeks 8 to 12. Paroxysmal coughing gradually decreases.

Classic clueSevere hacking cough followed by a high-pitched inspiratory whoop explains the names whooping cough and hundred-day cough.
Prevention
  • The lecture lists the DPT-Hib vaccine schedule at 2, 4, 6, and 15 to 18 months.
  • Protection is not lifelong.
  • Droplet control and reduction of close exposure are important because humans are the reservoir.
Legionella pneumophila Non-Enteric pp. 7–8

Structure and culture

  • Poorly staining Gram-negative rod.
  • May require silver stain rather than routine Gram stain.
  • Has a single polar flagellum.
  • Facultative intracellular organism found inside white cells or outside cells.
  • Fastidious and requires L-cysteine.
  • Grows on charcoal yeast extract medium.
  • Charcoal acts as a detoxifying agent.
  • Colonies may require several days to two weeks.
  • Catalase positive, oxidase positive, and urease negative in the lecture.

Environmental reservoir

  • Found in lakes, stagnant pools, fountains, ponds, and other environmental waters.
  • Lives within protozoa.
  • Can persist in cooling towers, air-conditioning systems, humidifiers, whirlpool spas, hot-water systems, and misting equipment.
  • Thrives at approximately 25°C to 42°C.
  • Transmission occurs by inhalation of contaminated aerosol.
  • The lecture notes that aerosol can travel far from the source.

Intracellular survival

  • Enters the macrophage and forms a Legionella-containing vacuole.
  • Inhibits fusion of the phagosome and lysosome.
  • Multiplies inside the protected vacuole.
  • Escapes and returns to the environment.
  • Can form a biofilm outside the host.

Diagnosis

  • Culture on charcoal yeast extract or CYE agar.
  • Indirect fluorescent antibody is listed.
  • ELISA is listed.
  • PCR is listed.
  • Exposure to a water-aerosol source provides an important epidemiologic clue.

Two clinical forms

FormClinical pattern
Legionnaires disease
  • Acute atypical pneumonia.
  • Nonproductive cough.
  • High fever and malaise.
  • Mild cough may occur despite significant disease.
  • Neurologic manifestations and encephalopathy are listed.
  • Chest radiograph may show a patchy infiltrate involving one lobe.
Pontiac fever
  • Acute nonfatal respiratory illness.
  • Mild flu-like symptoms.
  • Cough and headache.
  • No pneumonia is emphasized in the comparison.
Do not confuseLegionnaires disease includes pneumonia. Pontiac fever is a milder flu-like illness without pneumonia.

Bartonella species

SpeciesReservoir or vectorDisease and mechanismLaboratory and lecture treatment
Bartonella quintana
  • Human body louse, Pediculus corporis.
  • Transmission occurs when contaminated louse feces enter a bite wound.
  • Associated with crowding, poor sanitation, homelessness, and the historical trench setting.
Trench fever.
  • Blood and lymph-node aspirate may be collected.
  • Warthin-Starry stain is listed.
  • Semisolid agar with hemoglobin and rabbit serum may require ten days at 28°C.
  • PCR and ELISA are listed.
  • The lecture lists ampicillin, doxycycline, and ciprofloxacin.
Bartonella henselae
  • Cat reservoir and cat flea association.
  • Cat scratch or related exposure.
  • Cat-scratch disease in immunocompetent patients, often with lymphadenopathy.
  • Bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, affecting small blood vessels.
Bartonella bacilliformis
  • Sandfly vector.
  • Endemic setting in Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia in the lecture.
  • Oroya fever.
  • Acute hemolytic bacteremia.
  • Invasion of red blood cells produces fever and anemia.
Shared Bartonella virulence
  • Surface proteins support adherence to red blood cells.
  • Flagella support invasion of red blood cells and endothelial cells.

Pasteurella multocida

Characteristics

  • Gram-negative coccobacillus.
  • Nonmotile.
  • Facultative anaerobe.
  • Has a safety-pin appearance.
  • Oxidase positive.
  • Catalase positive.

Exposure and disease

  • Zoonotic organism carried by horses, cats, dogs, chickens, and sheep.
  • Cat or dog bite may produce rapidly developing cellulitis.
  • Inhalation is linked with meningitis and pneumonia in the lecture.
  • Specimens include wound swab, cerebrospinal fluid, and secretions.
  • Culture uses chocolate agar and blood agar.
Yersinia pestis and plague Non-Enteric pp. 9–10

Identity

  • Enteric organism discussed in the non-GIT enteric section.
  • Causative agent of plague and historically associated with the Black Death.
  • Classified as a Category A pathogen in the lecture.
  • Shows bipolar safety-pin staining.
  • Facultative intracellular organism.
  • Capsulated in young cultures and animal tissues.
  • Grows at approximately 27°C.

Major virulence factors

  • Yop virulon injects bacterial proteins and kills phagocytes.
  • F1 antigen is a capsular antigen produced at 37°C.
  • V and W antigens are produced intracellularly and protect against macrophage killing.
  • Pesticin is a bacteriocin.
  • Coagulase is produced inside the rat flea.
  • Fibrinolysin breaks down fibrin in human blood clots.

Plasmids

  • pPla activates plasminogen in the human host and is important in pneumonic plague.
  • pFra encodes phospholipase D and supports flea transmission.
  • The plasmids work with a pathogenicity island involved in adhesion, injection of bacterial proteins, and iron acquisition.

Transmission cycles

  • Rural plague involves rats and fleas.
  • Urban plague occurs when infected fleas transmit the organism from rats to humans.
  • Inhalation produces pneumonic plague.
  • An infected person may spread pneumonic disease through coughing, sneezing, and direct contact with infected tissue.

Clinical manifestations

FormLecture descriptionMain danger
Bubonic plague
  • Affects the lymphatic system.
  • Produces enlarged lymph nodes or buboes.
  • Small pustules or ulceration may occur.
Progression to systemic disease.
Septicemic plague
  • Affects the circulatory system.
  • Bleeding may occur under the skin and in internal organs.
  • Produces DIC, small-vessel necrosis, and purpura.
  • Acral regions such as fingers, toes, and nose may be affected.
Shock, widespread necrosis, and death.
Pneumonic plague
  • Affects the lungs.
  • May progress rapidly to cyanosis, respiratory failure, and septicemia.
  • The lecture emphasizes a critical 24-hour untreated period.
Rapidly fatal pneumonia and person-to-person droplet spread.

Diagnosis and treatment

  • Culture on MacConkey agar is listed.
  • Serology can detect antibodies against the F1 antigen.
  • PCR is listed for confirmation.
  • The lecture lists streptomycin.
  • The lecture also lists chloramphenicol.

If you see this cluster

Flea or rodent exposure + safety-pin organism + painful lymph-node enlargement means bubonic plague until proven otherwise. Pulmonary disease adds a droplet-transmission emergency.

Curved Gram-negative rods

Campylobacter jejuni GP Rods pp. 8–9

Identity

  • Curved or S-shaped Gram-negative rod.
  • May appear as seagull-wing pairs.
  • Motile.
  • Oxidase positive.
  • Microaerophilic.
  • Can grow at 42°C.

Exposure

  • Associated with poultry.
  • May follow unpasteurized milk.
  • May follow contaminated food or water.
  • Animal reservoirs are emphasized in the lecture.

Disease

  • Gastroenteritis with abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhea.
  • Stool may be watery or bloody.
  • Postinfectious Guillain-Barré syndrome is an important complication.
  • Reactive complications may follow infection.

Diagnosis

  • Stool specimen.
  • Selective culture under microaerophilic conditions.
  • Incubation at 42°C helps separate it from other curved rods.
  • Oxidase reaction supports identification.
Helicobacter pylori GP Rods pp. 9–10

Identity

  • Curved Gram-negative gastric rod.
  • Motile with flagella.
  • Microaerophilic.
  • Strongly urease positive.
  • Adapted to the mucus layer of the stomach.

Pathogenesis

  • Flagella help the organism move through gastric mucus.
  • Urease splits urea and helps create a less acidic local environment.
  • Attachment and persistent inflammation injure gastric mucosa.
  • Chronic colonization supports gastritis and ulcer formation.

Clinical associations

  • Chronic gastritis.
  • Peptic-ulcer disease.
  • Recurrent upper-abdominal symptoms in the lecture context.
  • Long-term association with gastric malignancy is included in the lecture.

Diagnosis and management

  • Rapid urease testing is a major laboratory clue.
  • Histologic and culture-based methods are discussed in the lecture.
  • Combination eradication therapy is required rather than a single drug.
  • Confirmation of eradication is included as a follow-up step.
Vibrio species GP Rods pp. 10–11
SpeciesIdentity and exposureVirulence and diseaseLaboratory and management clue
Vibrio cholerae
  • Curved comma-shaped Gram-negative rod.
  • Motile and oxidase positive.
  • Epidemic serogroups include O1 and O139 in the lecture.
  • Transmission occurs through contaminated food or water.
  • Lower gastric acidity increases susceptibility.
  • Cholera toxin has A and B components.
  • Raises intracellular cAMP and causes massive secretion of water and electrolytes.
  • TCP supports attachment.
  • Produces profuse watery or rice-water stool.
  • Rapid dehydration and hypovolemic shock are the major emergencies.
  • TCBS produces yellow colonies because of sucrose fermentation.
  • Rehydration is the first and most important treatment principle.
  • Clean water, sanitation, and food hygiene prevent transmission.
Vibrio parahaemolyticus
  • Halophilic marine organism.
  • Associated with seafood.
  • TDH and TRH are emphasized.
  • Causes seafood-associated gastroenteritis.
  • The lecture describes meat-wash stool.
  • Kanagawa phenomenon on Wagatsuma agar.
  • Does not ferment sucrose, so TCBS is not yellow.
Vibrio vulnificus
  • Halophilic marine Vibrio.
  • Exposure through raw seafood or coastal seawater.
  • Capsule is an important virulence factor.
  • Wound cellulitis and severe soft-tissue infection.
  • Septicemia after seafood exposure.
  • Liver disease is a major vulnerability clue in the lecture.
Culture plus a careful marine-exposure history supports identification.
Vibrio alginolyticusMarine halophilic organism.Associated with marine wound and ear infection.Culture and biochemical differentiation from the other Vibrio species.
Fast separation
  • Yellow TCBS + rice-water stool points to V. cholerae.
  • Seafood gastroenteritis + Kanagawa phenomenon points to V. parahaemolyticus.
  • Raw oyster or seawater + wound disease or septicemia in liver disease points to V. vulnificus.
Lesson 1.11

Anaerobes

The lecture approaches anaerobic disease through three linked questions. Why can the organism survive in the site, how did normal flora reach a normally sterile area, and was the specimen protected from oxygen during collection and transport?

Anaerobes pp. 1–14
Learning-objective map
  • Compare the oxygen requirements of aerobic, facultative, microaerophilic, aerotolerant, and obligately anaerobic organisms.
  • Correlate the virulence factors of the Clostridia with the characteristic clinical manifestations.
  • Discuss the pathogenesis of the anaerobic infections emphasized in the lecture.
  • Recognize the predisposing factors needed for endogenous anaerobic infection.
  • Interpret specimen collection, oxygen-free transport, culture conditions, indicators, special media, and biochemical results.

Oxygen biology

Aerobic or facultative organismAnaerobic organism
  • Uses cytochrome systems for oxygen metabolism.
  • Cytochromes transfer electrons in metabolic pathways, especially cellular respiration.
  • Does not have the same cytochrome systems for oxygen metabolism.
  • Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
  • May or may not have catalase.
  • Obligate anaerobes commonly lack enough catalase to resist oxygen injury.
  • Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide radicals into less toxic products.
  • Has low levels of superoxide dismutase.
  • Obligate anaerobes are susceptible to superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals.
Obligate anaerobes
  • Usually lack sufficient superoxide dismutase and catalase.
  • Are injured or killed by oxygen.
  • Grow best in a very low oxidation-reduction or redox environment.

Oxygen-requirement framework

CategoryWhere growth occursLecture example
Obligate aerobeNear atmospheric oxygen, approximately 20% to 21%.Mycobacterium tuberculosis
MicroaerophileAt a lower oxygen concentration, approximately 5%.Helicobacter pylori
Facultative anaerobeCan grow with little oxygen and can also grow without oxygen.Enteric rods and staphylococci
Aerotolerant anaerobeDoes not use oxygen but can tolerate limited exposure.Campylobacter jejuni is placed here in the lecture framework.
Obligate anaerobeGrows where oxygen is absent.Clostridium tetani, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and Peptostreptococcus

Where anaerobes survive

Normal low-redox sites

  • Oropharynx.
  • Colon.
  • Deep skin appendages.
  • Female genital tract.
  • Other mucosal sites with dense mixed flora.

Pathologic low-redox sites

  • Devitalized tissue.
  • Ischemic tissue.
  • Necrotic tissue.
  • Abscess cavity.
  • Tissue with poor blood supply.
  • Sites containing a foreign body.

Why polymicrobial infection helps

  • Facultative organisms such as E. coli consume oxygen.
  • The local redox potential falls.
  • Obligate anaerobes can then multiply.
  • The final infection commonly contains more than one organism.
  • The lecture therefore describes anaerobic infection as commonly polymicrobial.

Exogenous and endogenous sources

SourceHow infection beginsExamples from the lecture
Exogenous
  • Organism enters through trauma.
  • Organism enters through ingestion.
  • The organism is not acting as the patient’s displaced normal flora.
  • Clostridium tetani.
  • Clostridium botulinum.
  • Fusobacterium necrophorum.
Endogenous
  • Normal flora leaves its usual habitat.
  • Trauma or surgery breaks a mucosal barrier.
  • Organisms reach a normally sterile, low-oxygen site.
  • Bacteroides fragilis.
  • Prevotella.
  • Porphyromonas.
  • Fusobacterium nucleatum.
  • Actinomyces.
  • Anaerobic cocci.

Normal anaerobic flora by site

Body siteLecture organismsImportant point
Skin
  • Cutibacterium acnes, previously called Propionibacterium acnes.
  • Peptostreptococcus.
Deep appendages and sebaceous follicles provide a low-oxygen environment.
Female genital tract
  • Porphyromonas.
  • Prevotella bivia and P. disiens.
  • Lactobacilli.
  • Clostridia.
Displacement may produce pelvic inflammatory disease and tubo-ovarian abscess.
Oral cavity
  • Porphyromonas.
  • Prevotella.
  • Fusobacterium nucleatum.
  • Actinomyces.
  • The lecture gives a ratio of approximately 100 anaerobes to 1 aerobe.
  • F. necrophorum is not presented as normal oral flora.
Colon
  • Bacteroides fragilis group.
  • Prevotella.
  • Fusobacterium nucleatum.
  • Clostridium perfringens and C. difficile.
  • Bifidobacterium and Eubacterium.
The lecture gives a ratio of approximately 1000 anaerobes to 1 aerobe.

Predisposing factors for endogenous infection

1

Barrier disruption
Trauma or surgery allows normal flora to leave a mucosal surface.

2

Reduced perfusion
Vascular disease or tissue injury reduces blood and oxygen delivery.

3

Foreign material
A foreign body or device provides a protected surface and supports persistence.

4

Malignancy
Malignancy may obstruct, necrose, or weaken tissue and create a favorable site.

5

Facultative growth
Facultative bacteria consume remaining oxygen.

6

Anaerobic multiplication
Low redox potential, necrosis, and poor blood supply allow abscess-forming organisms to multiply.

Clinical clues to anaerobic infection

Location clues

  • Infection next to a mucosal surface.
  • Oral, dental, lung-aspiration, intra-abdominal, pelvic, and deep-tissue infection.
  • Human or animal bite.
  • Clenched-fist injury.

Appearance and odor clues

  • Foul-smelling discharge from short-chain fatty-acid metabolism.
  • Necrotic or gangrenous tissue.
  • Gas in tissue from carbon dioxide or hydrogen production.
  • Black-pigmented exudate from Prevotella or Porphyromonas.
  • Sulfur granules in actinomycotic drainage.

Laboratory and treatment clues

  • Abscess formation.
  • Bacteremia or endocarditis with no growth in routine aerobic blood culture.
  • Infection emerging after an antimicrobial drug that suppresses aerobes but not anaerobes.
  • The lecture gives aminoglycosides as an example of drugs that can leave anaerobic overgrowth unopposed.

Specimen collection and transport

PhaseCorrect practice from the lectureWhy it matters
Collection
  • Collect aseptically.
  • Use blood, abscess contents, deep-wound aspirate, needle aspirate, or normally sterile body fluid.
  • Suprapubic bladder aspiration is listed for urine.
  • Pleural, pericardial, cerebrospinal, peritoneal, and joint fluids are acceptable.
Deep aspirates and sterile-site material reduce contamination by surface flora.
Transport
  • Use an anaerobic disposable plastic bag with a resazurin indicator.
  • Use anaerobic fluid transport or an anaerobic transport kit.
  • Remove oxygen and heat-seal the bag.
  • Label whether the specimen is for aerobic or anaerobic work.
Oxygen exposure can kill the organism before culture.
Timing
  • Deliver the specimen promptly.
  • Notify the laboratory before collection when anaerobic processing is needed.
The laboratory can prepare the anaerobic glove box, media, and transport system.
ProcessingWork in an anaerobic glove box with a carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere as described in the lecture.Maintains the low-oxygen environment required for recovery.

Culture and identification

  • Anaerobes are difficult to isolate and may not be recovered even when infection is present.
  • Use blood agar supplemented with vitamin K and hemin.
  • Sheep blood may be included.
  • Selective antibiotics may be incorporated to test or select organisms such as Bacteroides.
  • Incubate for at least 48 hours and sometimes longer.
  • Use an anaerobic jar at approximately 35°C to 37°C.
  • An envelope containing sodium bicarbonate and sodium borohydride releases carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
  • Methylene blue is the anaerobic indicator.
  • The indicator becomes colorless when oxygen has been removed successfully.
  • Once a colony is recovered, commercially available biochemical tests may be used.
  • Gas-liquid chromatography can identify metabolic products.
  • Acetic acid is linked with Bifidobacterium.
  • Propionic acid is linked with Propionibacterium.
  • Isobutyric acid is linked with Porphyromonas.
  • Valeric acid is linked with Fusobacterium.
  • Isocaproic acid is linked with Peptostreptococcus.
Specimen trapA superficial swab exposed to air may fail even when the patient has a true anaerobic infection. The collection method is part of the diagnosis.

Anaerobic cocci

OrganismMorphology and normal siteDisease pattern
Peptostreptococcus
  • Gram-positive coccus.
  • Spherical or sometimes ovoid.
  • May occur in pairs, tetrads, clumps, or chains.
  • Capsulated, fastidious, slow growing, difficult to isolate, and often overlooked.
  • Found in colon, mouth, skin, and genitourinary tract.
  • Can infect the central nervous system, head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, skin, bone, joint, and soft tissue.
  • Abscess is the characteristic manifestation.
  • Usually part of a polymicrobial infection.
  • May participate in generalized necrotizing soft-tissue infection.
PeptoniphilusNormal flora of colon, mouth, skin, and genitourinary tract.Mixed endogenous infection and abscess.
PeptococcusNormal flora of mouth, intestinal tract, and skin.Mixed endogenous infection.
Veillonella
  • Gram-negative anaerobic coccus.
  • Oxidase negative and catalase negative.
  • Contains lipopolysaccharide.
  • Nonmotile.
  • Normal flora of mouth and colon.
  • Uses lactate produced by viridans streptococci.
  • Participates in oral biofilm, dental plaque, and dental caries.
  • May cause osteomyelitis, pyelonephritis, meningitis, endocarditis, and hepatic abscess.

Anaerobic Gram-negative rods

General pathogenesis
  • Usually act as opportunistic pathogens.
  • Trauma or surgery breaks the mucosa.
  • The organisms invade and release collagenase, neuraminidase, capsule-related factors, heparinase, and other enzymes.
  • Common sites include oral and dental tissues, lungs, abdomen, female genital tract, soft tissue, and bone.
  • Important shared factors include fimbriae, hemagglutinin, lectins, superoxide dismutase, catalase, capsule, immunoglobulin proteases, lipopolysaccharide, and succinic acid.
Bacteroides fragilis Anaerobes pp. 4–5

Identity

  • Gram-negative pleomorphic rod.
  • Obligate anaerobe.
  • Abundant colon flora.
  • May appear as both long and short rods.
  • Produces vitamin K.
  • May possess catalase.
  • Bile resistant and able to grow in 20% bile.

Virulence factors

  • Fimbriae support attachment.
  • Capsule prevents phagocytosis and promotes abscess formation.
  • Enterotoxin produces diarrhea.
  • Lipopolysaccharide stimulates cytokines and abscess formation.
  • The lecture describes its LPS as less toxic than enteric LPS and emphasizes less fever.
  • Heat-labile toxin produces inflammation of intestinal epithelium.
  • Superoxide dismutase allows survival during limited oxygen exposure until growth is established.

Pathogenesis and disease

  • Normal colon flora becomes pathogenic after intestinal-wall disruption.
  • Triggers include surgery, trauma, acute appendicitis, and diverticulitis.
  • The most emphasized result is intra-abdominal infection with abscess formation.
  • May enter the bloodstream and cause bacteremia.
  • May cause pelvic inflammatory disease and ovarian abscess.

Laboratory identity

  • Grows on Bacteroides bile-esculin agar.
  • Bile resistance allows growth while many other organisms are inhibited.
  • Esculin hydrolysis produces dark colonies with brown-black halos.
  • Short-chain fatty-acid metabolism produces a foul odor.
  • The lecture describes it as the most common anaerobe isolated from blood culture.

If you see this cluster

Disrupted colon + intra-abdominal abscess + bile-resistant dark BBEA colony strongly suggests Bacteroides fragilis.

Prevotella

  • Includes P. melaninogenica, P. bivia, and P. disiens.
  • Found in oral cavity, colon, and female genital tract.
  • Short Gram-negative rod.
  • Capsulated.
  • Produces IgM, IgA, and IgG proteases.
  • Requires vitamin K and heme.
  • Bile sensitive.
  • Produces a brown-black pigment.
  • Shows brick-red fluorescence under ultraviolet light.
  • Participates in polymicrobial PID, tubo-ovarian abscess, cerebral abscess, and lung abscess.

Porphyromonas

  • Normal flora of upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, and urogenital tract.
  • Has fimbriae.
  • Has hemagglutinin.
  • Produces IgM, IgA, and IgG proteases.
  • Produces black pigment.
  • Shows brick-red fluorescence under ultraviolet light.
  • Important in periodontitis and mixed oral disease.

Fusobacterium

  • Fusiform or spindle-shaped Gram-negative anaerobic rod.
  • F. nucleatum is normal oral flora and participates in periodontal disease.
  • Lectin supports attachment.
  • Lipopolysaccharide and other factors contribute to inflammation.
  • F. necrophorum is presented as an exogenous organism.
  • F. necrophorum may produce Lemierre syndrome with oropharyngeal infection and internal-jugular septic thrombophlebitis.

Anaerobic Gram-positive non-spore-forming rods

Actinomyces Anaerobes pp. 7–8

Identity

  • Branching filamentous Gram-positive rod.
  • Anaerobic.
  • Non-spore forming.
  • Non-acid-fast, which helps separate it from Nocardia.
  • Normal flora of oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and female genital tract.

Pathogenesis

  • Requires disruption of a mucosal barrier.
  • Produces a slowly progressive, contiguous infection.
  • Forms dense bacterial colonies surrounded by inflammatory material.
  • Drainage may contain yellow sulfur granules.
  • Fibrosis and sinus-tract formation support chronic persistence.

Clinical forms

  • Cervicofacial disease or lumpy jaw.
  • Thoracic infection.
  • Abdominal infection.
  • Pelvic disease associated with an intrauterine device.
  • Chronic mass-like infection that may cross tissue planes.

Diagnosis and management

  • Collect deep tissue or aspirate rather than a surface swab.
  • Look for sulfur granules.
  • Culture anaerobically for a prolonged period.
  • Molar-tooth colonies are a classic culture description.
  • Management requires prolonged antimicrobial treatment, drainage, and removal of a contributing foreign body when present.

Cutibacterium acnes

  • Previously called Propionibacterium acnes.
  • Gram-positive anaerobic non-spore-forming rod.
  • Normal flora of deep skin follicles and sebaceous glands.
  • Uses the low-oxygen, lipid-rich environment of the pilosebaceous unit.
  • Participates in follicular obstruction, comedone formation, and inflammation in acne.
  • May also contaminate or infect implanted devices.
  • Interpretation depends on specimen depth and clinical context because it is normal skin flora.

Clostridia and sporulation

Vegetative form

  • Develops when moisture and nutrients are favorable.
  • Produces toxins responsible for disease.
  • Usually susceptible to oxygen because the major species are obligate anaerobes.

Spore form

  • Forms under unfavorable environmental conditions.
  • Contains the original genetic material.
  • Has multiple protective protein coats.
  • Resists heat, drying, ethyl alcohol, and many chemicals.
  • May remain viable in the environment for years.
  • Germinates when moisture and nutrients return.
SpeciesMain diseaseCentral toxin
Clostridium perfringensGas gangrene or myonecrosis and food poisoningAlpha toxin or lecithinase, plus enterotoxin
Clostridium tetaniTetanusTetanospasmin and tetanolysin
Clostridium botulinumBotulismBotulinum neurotoxin
Clostridium difficilePseudomembranous colitisToxin A and toxin B
Clostridium septicumNontraumatic myonecrosisToxin-mediated tissue destruction
Clostridium perfringens Anaerobes pp. 9–11

Characteristics

  • Short, thick Gram-positive rod with blunt ends.
  • Capsule is seen in infected tissue.
  • Weakly catalase positive in the lecture.
  • Lecithinase positive.
  • Grows rapidly on blood agar.
  • Produces a double zone of hemolysis.
  • Can grow at 45°C.
  • Spores are rarely seen in the vegetative cell.

Alpha toxin

  • Major virulence factor.
  • Has lecithinase or phospholipase-C activity.
  • Destroys red blood cells, fibroblasts, myocytes, platelets, and leukocytes.
  • Produces myonecrosis.
  • Contributes to hemolysis and black tissue necrosis.
  • Reduces blood supply and worsens the anaerobic environment.

Other virulence factors

  • Collagenase.
  • Hyaluronidase.
  • Fibrinolysin.
  • Hemagglutinin.
  • Hemolysin.
  • Enterotoxin in food poisoning.

Biotypes in the lecture

  • Type A produces alpha toxin.
  • Type B produces alpha, beta, and epsilon toxins.
  • Type C produces alpha and beta toxins.
  • Type D produces alpha and epsilon toxins.
  • Type E produces alpha and iota toxins.

Gas-gangrene sequence

1

Spores enter through trauma, a deep wound, or contaminated material during septic abortion.

2

Necrotic tissue and poor oxygenation permit germination into vegetative cells.

3

Alpha toxin and tissue-destroying enzymes lyse cells and produce necrosis.

4

Blood supply becomes blocked and oxygen delivery falls further.

5

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen accumulate, producing gas and crepitus.

6

Rapid myonecrosis, blackening, systemic toxicity, and possible shock follow.

Food poisoning

  • Ingestion of spores in contaminated food.
  • Spores germinate and release enterotoxin during sporulation.
  • Produces diarrhea and abdominal pain.
  • The lecture emphasizes absence of fever and absence of vomiting.

Laboratory identification

TestPositive lecture finding
Robertson cooked-meat brothFatty acids consume oxygen and support anaerobic survival before subculture.
Blood agarRapid growth with a double zone of hemolysis.
Nagler testAlpha-toxin lecithinase hydrolyzes egg-yolk lecithin on the side without antitoxin.
Litmus milkStormy clot reaction from lactose fermentation, acid, gas, casein clotting, and litmus reduction.

Treatment

  • Prompt removal of necrotic tissue.
  • Antitoxin therapy is listed.
  • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is listed.
  • High-dose penicillin G is listed.
  • Clindamycin and metronidazole are listed to kill the bacterium rather than neutralize toxin already bound to tissue.
  • Amputation may be required when tissue cannot be salvaged.
Emergency cueRapid severe pain, swelling, gas, crepitus, black necrotic tissue, and systemic toxicity after a contaminated wound means gas gangrene and urgent source control.
Clostridium tetani Anaerobes pp. 11–12

Identity and source

  • Not capsulated.
  • Has a terminal spore that produces a drumstick appearance.
  • Exogenously acquired rather than normal flora.
  • Found in soil contaminated by cattle or horse feces.
  • Enters through a puncture wound or other contaminated wound.
  • Incubation in the lecture ranges from 1 to 54 days.

Toxins

  • Tetanolysin helps bacterial spread.
  • Tetanospasmin is the neurotoxin responsible for the clinical manifestations.
  • Tetanospasmin is encoded on a plasmid.

Pathogenesis

  • Necrotic anaerobic tissue permits spore germination.
  • Tetanospasmin travels along nerves toward the central nervous system.
  • Binds to neuronal structures, including the synaptobrevin-related system described in the lecture.
  • Suppresses release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine.
  • Loss of inhibition produces persistent muscle contraction and spasm.

Clinical manifestations

  • Trismus or lockjaw.
  • Risus sardonicus or devil’s grin.
  • Neck and generalized muscular rigidity.
  • Dysphagia.
  • Painful spasms.
  • Opisthotonic posturing.
  • Autonomic nervous-system instability, which the lecture identifies as a major cause of death.

Diagnosis and treatment

  • Laboratory recovery uses the same anaerobic approach as C. perfringens.
  • Robertson cooked-meat broth may be followed by blood-agar culture.
  • Small flat translucent colonies with a narrow zone of hemolysis are described.
  • Give human tetanus immunoglobulin immediately to neutralize unbound toxin.
  • Give tetanus toxoid because disease does not provide reliable active immunity.
  • Control spasms.
  • Perform aggressive wound care.
  • Use metronidazole to stop bacterial growth.
  • Provide airway and ventilatory support when needed.
Mechanism cueLoss of GABA and glycine release produces spastic paralysis. This is the opposite of the flaccid paralysis caused by botulinum toxin.
Clostridium botulinum Anaerobes pp. 12–13

Identity and source

  • Has a subterminal spore.
  • Exogenously acquired and not normal flora.
  • Lives in animal intestines and survives in soil.
  • Toxin types listed are A, B, C, C2, D, E, F, and G.
  • Types A, B, and E are emphasized as human disease types.
  • Type A is presented as the most potent.
  • The lecture notes that toxin is released after bacterial death.

Four clinical forms

  • Foodborne botulism after home-preserved food.
  • Wound botulism after wound contamination, including injection-related wounds.
  • Infant botulism after ingestion of spores in honey.
  • Iatrogenic botulism after excessive therapeutic or cosmetic toxin exposure.

Food conditions

  • Improperly canned food with low oxygen.
  • Low acidity and a pH above 4.6 favor toxin production.
  • High water content.
  • Warning signs include loose, swollen, or dented lids, cracked jars, abnormal fluid, and an off odor.

Mechanism

  • Toxin is endocytosed at the nerve terminal.
  • The light chain cleaves specific SNARE proteins.
  • The SNARE complex does not form.
  • Synaptic vesicles cannot fuse with the terminal membrane.
  • Acetylcholine is not released.
  • Muscle fibers cannot contract, producing flaccid paralysis.

Clinical manifestations

  • Weakness of the eye muscles.
  • Drooping eyelids.
  • Large nonmoving pupils.
  • Double vision.
  • Trouble speaking.
  • Trouble swallowing.
  • Trouble breathing.
  • Symmetric descending weakness and respiratory paralysis.
  • Infants may develop constipation, poor feeding, and hypotonia.

Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention

  • Heat or alcohol may be used to suppress other organisms before plating because the spore is resistant.
  • Culture uses Robertson cooked-meat broth and blood agar after three to five days.
  • The lecture lists trivalent antitoxin for adults.
  • Human botulism immunoglobulin is listed for infants.
  • Penicillin G is listed for wound botulism.
  • Mechanical ventilation may be lifesaving.
  • Inspect canned food before use.
  • Keep cooked food hot at 60°C or cold at 4°C.
  • Cook and reheat food thoroughly because the toxin is heat-labile.
  • Do not give honey to children younger than one year.
Emergency cueEarly cranial-nerve symptoms followed by descending flaccid paralysis means botulism and possible respiratory failure.
Clostridium difficile Anaerobes pp. 13–14

Ecology and trigger

  • May be present as normal flora.
  • Important healthcare-associated infection.
  • Spores persist in the environment.
  • Prolonged antimicrobial treatment suppresses competing facultative flora.
  • The lecture lists clindamycin, ampicillin, beta-lactams, and fluoroquinolones as triggers.
  • Loss of competing flora permits overgrowth and toxin release.

Toxin A

  • Also called TcdA or enterotoxin.
  • Produces diarrhea.
  • Attracts neutrophils.
  • Increases intestinal hemorrhage and fluid secretion.

Toxin B

  • Also called TcdB or cytotoxin.
  • Inactivates Rho proteins.
  • Destroys the cytoskeleton and intestinal epithelium.
  • Produces mucosal necrosis with inflammatory cells and fibrin.

Pseudomembrane

  • Accumulation of inflammatory cells and fibrin forms a pseudomembrane.
  • Appears as whitish plaques on colonoscopy.
  • Severe disease may progress to toxic megacolon.

Laboratory diagnosis

MethodLecture result
Cycloserine-cefoxitin-fructose agar
  • Yellow colonies from fructose fermentation.
  • Horse-manure odor.
  • Yellow-green fluorescence under ultraviolet light.
PCRDetection of the toxin-B gene in a stool specimen.
Cytotoxin tissue-culture assay
  • Vero-cell tissue culture is described as the standard diagnostic method in the lecture.
  • Cellular change and lysis demonstrate toxin activity.
Central sequenceAntimicrobial suppression of normal flora → C. difficile overgrowth → TcdA and TcdB release → epithelial injury → neutrophils and fibrin → pseudomembranous colitis.
Control principles
  • Use contact and spore-focused infection-control measures.
  • Clean the environment.
  • Practice hand hygiene.
  • Use antimicrobial stewardship to reduce unnecessary disruption of normal flora.
Spastic versus flaccid paralysis
  • Tetanus blocks inhibitory GABA and glycine release. The result is rigidity and spastic paralysis.
  • Botulism blocks acetylcholine release. The result is descending flaccid paralysis.
Lesson 1.12

Spirochetes and Atypical Bacteria

These organisms require a different diagnostic approach because they may be too thin for routine stains, unable to grow on ordinary media, missing a cell wall, or dependent on an intracellular developmental cycle. The correct specimen and test often change with the stage of disease.

Spirochetes and Atypicals pp. 1–17
Learning-objective map
  • Describe the characteristics of atypical bacteria.
  • Correlate pathophysiology with the clinical manifestations caused by atypical bacteria.
  • Analyze the diagnostic methods appropriate for each organism and stage of infection.
  • Formulate the lecture-supported treatment and preventive plan.
  • Describe medically important spirochetes by morphology, virulence, and growth characteristics.
  • Discuss the pathogenesis of syphilis, relapsing fever, Lyme disease, and leptospirosis.
  • Differentiate medically important Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Coxiella, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia.

Spirochete structure

  • Long, slender, helically coiled, spiral, or corkscrew-shaped bacilli.
  • Gram-negative structural organization.
  • Motile because of internal axial filaments rather than external flagella.
  • Medically important genera are Treponema, Borrelia, and Leptospira.
  • The outer sheath is a glycosaminoglycan coating.
  • An outer membrane lies inside the sheath.
  • Peptidoglycan supports structural integrity.
  • Endoflagella or axial filaments lie in the periplasmic space and wind around the protoplasmic cylinder.
  • The inner membrane provides osmotic stability.
  • Cytoplasmic tubules or body fibrils lie near the inner membrane.
Treponema pallidum and syphilis Spirochetes pp. 1–3

Morphology and growth

  • Long slender spiral approximately 0.2 μm wide and 5 to 15 μm long.
  • Regularly spaced coils.
  • Actively motile and rotates around the endoflagella.
  • May remain attached to host cells by tapered ends.
  • Too thin for routine light microscopy and ordinary aniline stains.
  • Can be seen with dark-field illumination, immunofluorescence, or silver impregnation.
  • Has never been continuously cultured on ordinary artificial media, fertile eggs, or routine tissue culture.
  • Drying and heat kill the organism rapidly.

Antigens and virulence

  • Outer-membrane proteins promote adherence to host cells.
  • Hyaluronidase breaks down hyaluronic acid and supports tissue invasion and perivascular infiltration.
  • Fibronectin coating helps prevent phagocytosis by macrophages.
  • Membrane proteins contain lipid components that help anchor them and limit antibody access.
  • Cardiolipin participates in the antibody response used by nontreponemal tests.
  • The infection produces both reagin antibodies and antibodies directed against treponemal antigens.

Entry and spread

  • Usually transmitted by sexual contact.
  • Penetrates intact mucous membrane or enters through a break in the epidermis.
  • Multiplies at the entry site.
  • Spreads to nearby lymph nodes.
  • Reaches the bloodstream and disseminates early.
  • Inflammation is rich in lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Specimens

  • Early surface lesion fluid for direct demonstration by dark-field microscopy or immunofluorescence.
  • Lesion material for nucleic-acid amplification when available.
  • Blood for serologic tests.
  • Cerebrospinal fluid for VDRL when neurosyphilis is being assessed.

Stages of acquired syphilis

StageClinical manifestationsPathogenesis and infectivity
Initial contact and primary syphilis
  • A papule develops at the site of inoculation.
  • The papule breaks down into a painless ulcer with a clean, hard base.
  • This hard chancre is the primary lesion.
  • Some lesions are intrarectal, perianal, or oral and may be missed.
  • The lesion heals spontaneously after weeks even without treatment.
  • Organisms multiply locally.
  • Spread to lymph nodes and blood occurs early.
  • The lesion contains many spirochetes and is infectious.
Secondary syphilis
  • Red maculopapular rash may involve any body area.
  • Palms and soles are characteristically involved.
  • Moist pale papules or condylomata lata occur in anogenital, axillary, or oral areas.
  • May cause meningitis, chorioretinitis, hepatitis, nephritis, or periostitis.
  • Systemic symptoms accompany dissemination.
  • Widespread multiplication produces lesions in skin and mucosa.
  • Primary and secondary lesions are rich in organisms.
  • These stages are highly infectious.
  • Contagious lesions may recur during the first several years.
Latent syphilis
  • No clinical signs or symptoms.
  • Detected mainly by a positive serologic test.
  • Some untreated cases resolve spontaneously.
  • Some remain latent.
  • Others later progress to tertiary disease.
Tertiary syphilis
  • Gummatous lesions in skin, bone, or liver.
  • Meningovascular syphilis.
  • Paresis and tabes dorsalis.
  • Aortitis, aortic aneurysm, and aortic-valve insufficiency.
  • Treponemes are rare in tertiary lesions.
  • Tissue injury is linked to an exaggerated hypersensitivity response.

Congenital syphilis

Transmission and fetal outcome

  • Transplacental spread can begin around 10 to 15 weeks of gestation in the lecture.
  • May cause miscarriage.
  • May cause stillbirth.
  • Some infected infants are born alive and develop manifestations later.
  • Adequate maternal treatment during pregnancy prevents congenital syphilis.

Childhood manifestations

  • Interstitial keratitis.
  • Hutchinson teeth.
  • Saddle nose.
  • Periostitis.
  • Central-nervous-system abnormalities.
  • Active congenital infection produces infant IgM antitreponemal antibody.

Serologic diagnosis

Test groupExamplesWhat it detects and how it is usedLimitations
NontreponemalRPR, VDRL, TRUST
  • Detects reagin activity against cardiolipin-related antigen.
  • Used as a screening test.
  • Can be reported quantitatively.
  • Useful for following response to therapy.
  • VDRL is standardized for cerebrospinal fluid.
  • May remain negative during very early infection.
  • False-positive reactions occur in other conditions.
  • Prozone phenomenon can cause a false-negative result when antibody is excessive.
  • Persistent or rising titer after treatment suggests failure or reinfection.
TreponemalTP-PA, THPA, MHA-TP, FTA-ABS, EIA, CIA
  • Detects antibodies against T. pallidum antigens.
  • Confirms whether a positive screening test is truly treponemal.
  • TP-PA uses sensitized gelatin particles.
  • Hemagglutination tests use sensitized sheep erythrocytes.
  • FTA-ABS uses indirect immunofluorescence.
  • Often remains positive for life after infection.
  • Less useful for following treatment response.
  • Hemagglutination methods may have nonspecific agglutination.

Treatment and prevention

  • Penicillin is the treatment of choice in the lecture.
  • Syphilis of less than one year is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly.
  • Older or latent disease is treated with benzathine penicillin G once weekly for three weeks.
  • Neurosyphilis is treated with intravenous penicillin G.
  • Evaluate the patient for other sexually transmitted infections.
  • Evaluate and treat sexual partners.
  • Prevent transmission through prompt case treatment, contact follow-up, abstinence, monogamy, and correct condom use.
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
  • Acute self-limited febrile reaction within 24 hours after treatment of a spirochetal infection.
  • Caused by release of products from dying organisms.
  • Most common after treatment of early syphilis.
  • May cause fever, headache, myalgia, rigors, diaphoresis, hypotension, and transient worsening of rash.
  • Pregnancy may be complicated by uterine contractions.

If you see this sequence

Painless hard chancre → palms-and-soles rash or condyloma lata → asymptomatic latency → neurologic, aortic, or gummatous disease is the classic syphilis progression.

Borrelia species

Relapsing fever Spirochetes pp. 3–4

Epidemic relapsing fever

  • Caused by Borrelia recurrentis.
  • Transmitted by the human body louse.
  • Infection follows rubbing of crushed lice or contaminated material into a bite site.

Endemic relapsing fever

  • Transmitted by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros.
  • B. hermsii is transmitted by O. hermsi.
  • Rodents are the main reservoir.

Borrelia miyamotoi

  • Transmitted by Ixodes scapularis.
  • May produce a Lyme-like febrile illness.
  • High fever, fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and nausea are listed.
  • Typical erythema migrans is absent.

Morphology and antigenic variation

  • Irregular spirals approximately 10 to 30 μm long.
  • Stain with Giemsa or Wright stain.
  • Can be cultivated in fluid media containing blood, serum, or tissue.
  • May survive for months at 4°C.
  • Surface antigens change during a single infection.
  • Antibody clears the dominant antigenic population.
  • A different antigenic variant survives and multiplies.
  • The host must generate a new antibody response.
  • This repeated escape produces recurrent fever cycles.

Clinical cycle

1

Incubation
Approximately 3 to 10 days.

2

Febrile stage
Sudden fever, chills, severe headache, and malaise. Organisms are present in blood.

3

Antibody response
Antibodies clear the current antigenic variant.

4

Afebrile stage
Lasts several days. Organisms are not detected and the patient is weak but less ill.

5

Variant emergence
A new antigenic type multiplies.

6

Relapse
Another fever episode occurs, often with decreasing severity over repeated cycles.

Diagnosis and control

  • Collect blood during the rise in fever when organisms are present.
  • Use thin or thick smears stained with Wright or Giemsa.
  • ELISA or immunofluorescence may detect antibodies after approximately one week.
  • PCR and molecular typing are listed.
  • The lecture lists tetracycline, erythromycin, and penicillin.
  • Prevent endemic disease by avoiding ticks.
  • Prevent epidemic disease by delousing, cleanliness, insecticides, and washing contaminated clothing or fomites.
Borrelia burgdorferi and Lyme disease Spirochetes pp. 4–5

Identity and vector

  • Spiral organism approximately 20 to 30 μm long.
  • Has multiple endoflagella and is highly motile.
  • Transmitted by Ixodes ticks.
  • Can be isolated from erythema-migrans skin lesions.
  • Animal reservoirs maintain the tick cycle.

Early localized disease

  • Erythema migrans develops at the bite site.
  • Expanding red lesion may have central clearing.
  • Fever, fatigue, headache, myalgia, or arthralgia may occur.

Disseminated and late disease

  • Neurologic involvement.
  • Cardiac involvement.
  • Multiple skin lesions may appear during dissemination.
  • Late arthritis is a major feature.

Diagnosis and treatment

  • Typical erythema migrans may permit clinical diagnosis.
  • Otherwise use an EIA or immunofluorescence screening approach followed by IgM or IgG immunoblot.
  • The lecture lists doxycycline, amoxicillin, cefuroxime, or ceftriaxone according to stage and manifestation.
  • Prevent through tick avoidance and prompt tick removal.
Leptospira and leptospirosis Spirochetes pp. 5–7

Morphology and reservoir

  • Thin tightly coiled spirochete with a hooked end.
  • Aerobic and actively motile.
  • Animals carry the organism in renal tubules.
  • Organisms are shed in urine.
  • Floodwater, stagnant water, soil, and farm runoff become contaminated.

Transmission

  • Enters through cuts, abrasions, or other skin breaks.
  • Can enter through conjunctiva or other mucous membrane.
  • Risk increases with wading, swimming, rescue work, or prolonged residence in flooded areas.
  • Rainy-season exposure is a major Philippine context.

Biphasic pathogenesis

  • Leptospiremic phase has organisms in blood and cerebrospinal fluid.
  • Immune phase follows antibody production.
  • During the immune phase, organisms may be recovered from urine.
  • Vascular injury and multiorgan inflammation explain renal, hepatic, hemorrhagic, and meningeal disease.

Clinical clues

  • Fever and headache.
  • Severe myalgia, especially calf tenderness.
  • Conjunctival suffusion.
  • May be anicteric and self-limited.
  • Severe Weil disease includes jaundice, renal failure, bleeding, and systemic compromise.
  • Aseptic meningitis may occur.

Diagnosis by stage

StageBest specimen and test concept
Early leptospiremic phase
  • Blood and cerebrospinal fluid.
  • Direct detection, culture, or PCR before antibody is fully developed.
Immune phase
  • Urine may contain organisms.
  • IgM serology becomes useful.
  • Microscopic agglutination test or MAT is the reference serologic method in the lecture.

Treatment and prevention

  • The lecture lists doxycycline for milder disease.
  • The lecture lists intravenous penicillin G for severe disease.
  • Avoid floodwater, stagnant water, and animal-farm runoff when possible.
  • Wear protective boots and gloves.
  • Cover wounds.
  • Control rodents and protect food from contamination.
  • Doxycycline is the listed post-exposure prophylactic agent.
  • The prophylaxis schedule depends on whether exposure is single, repeated, associated with wounds, or involves ingestion.
Exposure category in lectureExampleDoxycycline schedule listed
Low riskSingle wading exposure without wound or open lesion.200 mg single dose within 24 to 72 hours.
Moderate riskSingle exposure with wound, open lesion, or accidental ingestion.200 mg once daily for 3 to 5 days, started within 24 to 72 hours.
High riskContinuous or repeated exposure, including residents, rescuers, or relief workers.200 mg once weekly until exposure ends.

If you see this cluster

Floodwater or animal-urine exposure + calf tenderness + conjunctival suffusion strongly suggests leptospirosis. Jaundice and renal failure indicate severe disease.

Mycoplasma

Defining structural difference
  • Smallest free-living bacteria in the lecture.
  • Can pass through filters with approximately 450-nm pores.
  • Lacks a rigid cell wall and peptidoglycan.
  • Cell membrane contains sterols.
  • Highly pleomorphic and osmotically fragile.
  • Does not stain reliably with the Gram method.
  • Completely resistant to beta-lactam drugs because there is no cell-wall target.
  • Many species colonize the mouth, respiratory tract, or genitourinary tract.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae Atypicals pp. 8–9

Epidemiology

  • Endemic worldwide.
  • Transmitted by respiratory secretions and fomites.
  • Close shared spaces facilitate spread.
  • Schoolchildren, young adults, and military recruits are emphasized.
  • Grows better in aerobic respiratory environments even though it is described as facultatively anaerobic.

Attachment

  • Inhaled in respiratory droplets.
  • Uses a specialized attachment organelle.
  • P1 adhesin binds to respiratory epithelial cells.
  • Firm attachment prevents effective mucociliary removal.

Tissue injury

  • Releases lytic enzymes.
  • Releases superoxide.
  • Releases hydrogen peroxide.
  • Multiplies on the respiratory epithelium.
  • Damages ciliated cells and reduces mucociliary clearance.
  • Macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes contribute to inflammation.

Clinical manifestations

  • May be asymptomatic.
  • Insidious malaise, fever, headache, sore throat, and dry hacking cough.
  • Produces atypical or walking pneumonia.
  • Chest radiograph may show patchy interstitial infiltrates despite mild bedside appearance.
  • May be followed by encephalitis in children.
  • Other associations listed include erythema multiforme, neuritis, myocarditis, pericarditis, arthritis, and pancreatitis.

Diagnosis

  • Chest radiograph shows patchy infiltrates.
  • Sputum can be cultured on Eaton agar rich in cholesterol and nucleic acids.
  • Growth may take two to four weeks, so culture is not commonly used.
  • Colonies may be dome-shaped. The classic fried-egg appearance is less obvious than in M. hominis.
  • PCR is the test of choice in the lecture.
  • Cold agglutinins may support diagnosis.
  • IgM cross-reacts with red-cell antigen at 4°C and causes clumping.
  • A negative cold-agglutinin test does not exclude disease.
  • A titer of at least 1:64 supports the diagnosis.

Treatment

  • Beta-lactams are ineffective.
  • The lecture lists tetracyclines.
  • The lecture lists macrolides such as erythromycin and azithromycin.
  • The lecture lists fluoroquinolones.

Genitourinary Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma

OrganismCharacteristicsClinical associations
Mycoplasma hominis
  • Facultative anaerobe.
  • Can colonize the genitourinary tract.
  • Can be recovered from asymptomatic people.
  • Produces a dome-shaped or fried-egg colony.
  • Upper urinary-tract infection and pyelonephritis.
  • Salpingitis.
  • Tubo-ovarian abscess and pelvic inflammatory disease.
  • Postabortal and postpartum fever.
  • May be isolated from blood or joint fluid in disseminated disease.
Mycoplasma genitalium
  • Wall-less sexually transmitted organism.
  • Difficult to cultivate.
  • Molecular methods are important.
  • Nongonococcal urethritis.
  • Cervicitis.
  • Endometritis and salpingitis.
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility associations.
Ureaplasma urealyticum
  • Extremely small wall-less organism.
  • Requires urea for growth.
  • Urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
  • Often part of female perineal or vaginal flora.
  • Nongonococcal urethritis.
  • Genitourinary transmission.
  • Neonatal respiratory disease association.

Chlamydia

Core identity
  • Small Gram-negative-like obligate intracellular bacteria.
  • Cannot generate enough energy independently and depend on host cells.
  • Have a unique developmental cycle with two forms.
  • Do not grow on ordinary cell-free culture media.
  • Inclusions can be demonstrated with special stains and cell culture.
FormFunctionSequence
Elementary body
  • Small infectious extracellular form.
  • Survives long enough outside the cell to attach and enter.
  1. Elementary body attaches to the host cell.
  2. Host cell internalizes the organism.
  3. The elementary body reorganizes into a reticulate body.
  4. Reticulate bodies divide in an intracellular inclusion.
  5. They reorganize into new elementary bodies.
  6. Elementary bodies are released to infect new cells.
Reticulate body
  • Larger metabolically active intracellular form.
  • Replicates by binary fission.
  • Not the main infectious extracellular form.

Medically important Chlamydia

Organism or serovarDiseaseHigh-yield features
C. trachomatis A to CTrachoma
  • Chronic ocular infection.
  • Repeated inflammation and scarring can lead to visual impairment.
  • Community hygiene and treatment of cases and contacts are important.
C. trachomatis D to K
  • Nongonococcal urethritis.
  • Cervicitis.
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease.
  • Neonatal conjunctivitis.
  • Neonatal pneumonia.
  • Neonatal conjunctivitis appears approximately 5 to 12 days after birth.
  • Neonatal pneumonia may have a staccato cough.
  • NAAT is the major diagnostic method.
C. trachomatis L1 to L3Lymphogranuloma venereum
  • Transient initial genital lesion may be missed.
  • Painful regional lymph nodes and buboes follow.
  • Proctitis may occur.
  • A longer doxycycline course is listed.
C. pneumoniaeAtypical respiratory infectionMolecular and serologic diagnosis.
C. psittaciPsittacosis
  • Associated with birds and dried bird excreta.
  • Prevention includes control of bird shipment, quarantine, testing, and veterinary measures.

Treatment and prevention

  • Doxycycline is listed for nongonococcal urethritis and nonpregnant patients.
  • Azithromycin is effective and can be given during pregnancy.
  • Oral erythromycin is preferred in the lecture for neonatal pneumonia and neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis.
  • Topical eye therapy alone is not effective for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis.
  • Test and treat sexual contacts, including asymptomatic contacts.
  • Search for other sexually transmitted infections because coinfection is common.
  • Prevent neonatal disease by identifying and treating the pregnant patient and partner.

Rickettsia and related genera

Shared structural features

  • Pleomorphic nonmotile coccobacilli.
  • Weakly Gram-negative.
  • May require Giemsa, Gimenez, or Macchiavello stains.
  • Obligate intracellular organisms.
  • Depend on the host for energetic compounds such as coenzyme A and NAD.

Shared pathogenesis

  • Most are zoonotic and transmitted by ticks, mites, fleas, or lice.
  • OmpA and OmpB support adherence to endothelial cells.
  • Organisms multiply slowly inside endothelial cells.
  • Cell lysis releases organisms and exposes them to the immune system.
  • Vasculitis causes edema, rash, hemorrhage, thrombosis, tissue necrosis, and multiorgan complications.

Rickettsial disease comparison

Disease and organismVector or reservoirClinical pattern
Rocky Mountain spotted fever
R. rickettsii
  • Tick vector.
  • Maintained transovarially in ticks.
  • Dogs and small rodents may participate in the ecology.
  • Fever, headache, and myalgia.
  • After several days, rash begins on extremities and spreads centripetally.
  • Palms and soles are involved.
  • Severe vasculitis may produce pulmonary edema and hemorrhage.
Epidemic typhus
R. prowazekii		Human body louse
  • Severe systemic illness with fever lasting about two weeks.
  • Red macular rash begins on the trunk and spreads outward.
  • Hands, feet, and head are usually spared.
  • More severe in older adults.
  • Brill-Zinsser disease is late recrudescence from persistent infection.
Murine typhus
R. typhi		Rat flea, with infected feces rubbed into a bite wound
  • Resembles epidemic typhus.
  • Usually milder and rarely fatal except in elderly patients.
Rickettsialpox
R. akari		Bloodsucking mite associated with mice
  • Mild illness.
  • Papule at the bite site develops into a vesicle and black eschar.
  • Generalized vesicular rash may resemble varicella.
Scrub typhus
Orientia tsutsugamushi		Infected mites or chiggers, maintained transovarially
  • Resembles epidemic typhus.
  • Punched-out ulcer with a black eschar.
  • Generalized lymphadenopathy and lymphocytosis.
  • May become severe with cardiac or cerebral involvement.
Rash-direction comparison
  • RMSF begins on the extremities, moves inward, and involves palms and soles.
  • Epidemic typhus begins on the trunk, moves outward, and usually spares hands, feet, and head.

Coxiella, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia

OrganismDistinctive biologyDisease clue and diagnosis
Coxiella burnetii
  • Obligate intracellular organism.
  • Exception to the usual arthropod-transmission rule in this group.
  • Transmitted by inhalation of infected animal dust or aerosol.
  • Associated with livestock and birth products.
  • Causes Q fever.
  • May produce febrile illness, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis, or chronic endocarditis.
  • Serology and molecular tests are used.
  • Doxycycline is the lecture treatment anchor.
Anaplasma phagocytophilum
  • Tick-borne.
  • Invades granulocytes.
  • Forms intracellular morulae.
  • Fever, headache, myalgia, and laboratory cytopenias.
  • Rash is usually absent.
  • Smear, PCR, and serology are listed.
  • Doxycycline is used.
Ehrlichia chaffeensis
  • Tick-borne.
  • Invades monocytes.
  • Forms intracellular morulae.
  • Febrile systemic illness with cytopenias.
  • Rash is usually absent.
  • Smear, PCR, and serology are listed.
  • Doxycycline is used.
Cell mnemonic
  • Anaplasma goes to granulocytes.
  • Ehrlichia goes to monocytes.
  • Both may show morulae in the infected white-cell lineage.
Lesson 1.13

Mycobacteria

The mycobacterial cell wall explains almost everything important about the group. Mycolic acids create acid-fastness, slow nutrient exchange, clumping, environmental resistance, prolonged culture, and difficult antimicrobial penetration.

Mycobacteria pp. 1–15
Learning-objective map
  • Describe the nature, characteristics, and classification of Mycobacteria.
  • Recognize the Philippine and global disease burden described in the lecture.
  • Explain transmission, pathogenesis, cellular immune response, and delayed hypersensitivity.
  • Differentiate latent infection, active disease, primary tuberculosis, and reactivation tuberculosis.
  • Match the clinical pattern with AFB smear, culture, NAAT, TST, IGRA, and imaging.
  • Outline first-line treatment, multidrug rationale, resistance, directly observed therapy, and prevention.
  • Differentiate the tuberculosis complex, M. leprae, and nontuberculous mycobacteria.

General characteristics

  • Aerobic, non-spore-forming, nonmotile bacilli.
  • Slightly curved rods.
  • Not reliably classified as ordinary Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria.
  • The cell wall is fundamentally acid-fast.
  • High lipid content dominates the envelope.
  • Long-chain mycolic acids are linked to arabinogalactan and peptidoglycan.
  • The hydrophobic wall is difficult to penetrate with routine stains, disinfectants, and antimicrobial drugs.
  • Carbolfuchsin enters with heat or phenol.
  • Acid-alcohol cannot remove the retained dye from an intact mycolic-acid wall.
  • Damage to the wall reduces acid-fastness.

Growth and environmental resistance

Slow growth

  • M. tuberculosis has an approximately 18-hour doubling time.
  • This is much slower than the 20-minute doubling time used for E. coli comparison in the lecture.
  • Typical culture may require three to eight weeks.
  • Traditional culture may become positive only after several weeks.
  • Empiric therapy may begin before culture confirmation.
  • Slow multiplication explains the chronic clinical course.

Air hungry

  • Obligate aerobe.
  • Derives energy from oxidation of simple carbon compounds.
  • Growth is enhanced by increased carbon-dioxide tension.
  • Oxygen-rich lung apices are favored during reactivation tuberculosis.

Physical and chemical resistance

  • Hydrophobic waxy surface resists weak disinfectants.
  • Tendency to grow in clumps protects organisms.
  • Resistant to desiccation and may survive in dried sputum.
  • Harsh acid or alkali can suppress ordinary respiratory flora while tubercle bacilli survive specimen processing.
  • Heat through pasteurization and ultraviolet light can kill the organisms.

Staining and culture media

MethodResultLecture role
Ziehl-Neelsen stainRed acid-fast bacilli against a blue background.Classic widely available screening method.
Auramine-rhodamine fluorochrome stainYellow-orange fluorescent bacilli.
  • More sensitive for clinical specimens.
  • The lecture notes that it is not the routine Philippine method.
Middlebrook 7H10 or 7H11Defined semisynthetic agar.
  • Contains salts, oleic acid, albumin, catalase, and glycerol.
  • Useful for colony morphology and susceptibility testing.
Löwenstein-JensenEgg-based medium with malachite green.
  • Malachite green inhibits contaminants.
  • Small inocula may require three to six weeks.
Middlebrook 7H9 or MGITAutomated broth culture.
  • Tween disperses hydrophobic clumping.
  • Faster and more sensitive than classic solid culture.
  • Described as the laboratory workhorse.
Screening versus confirmation
  • Staining rapidly shows acid-fast bacilli.
  • Culture identifies the species and permits susceptibility testing.
  • A positive smear does not by itself prove that the organism is M. tuberculosis.

Classification and pathogenicity

GroupImportant organismsLecture concept
M. tuberculosis complexM. tuberculosis, M. bovis, and related complex members
  • M. tuberculosis is mainly respiratory.
  • M. bovis can infect humans through unpasteurized milk and produce gastrointestinal or extrapulmonary disease.
Leprosy organismM. lepraeObligate intracellular organism that targets macrophages and Schwann cells and prefers cooler tissues.
Nontuberculous mycobacteriaMAC, M. kansasii, M. ulcerans, M. marinum, rapid growers, and others
  • Mainly environmental organisms in soil and water.
  • Usually acquired from the environment rather than person-to-person spread.
  • Host immunity and structural lung disease determine the clinical pattern.
Infection is not the same as disease
  • An infected person may harbor the organism without symptoms.
  • Active disease means the person is ill and may be infectious.
  • Latent tuberculosis is contained and not contagious.
  • The carrier concept used for some organisms does not apply in the same way to tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis burden and risk

Global burden in the lecture

  • Approximately 10.6 million new cases per year.
  • Approximately 1.3 million deaths per year.
  • About one-fourth of the world population is estimated to have latent infection.
  • High burden in Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Western Pacific.
  • Poverty, crowding, malnutrition, HIV, diabetes, smoking, incarceration, homelessness, and immunosuppressive therapy increase risk.
  • MDR-TB and XDR-TB threaten control programs.

Philippine focus in the lecture

  • Presented as one of the highest-burden countries worldwide.
  • Severely endemic transmission.
  • High morbidity, mortality, MDR-TB, and TB-HIV burden.
  • Urban crowding, delayed care-seeking, self-medication, stigma, underdiagnosis, and poor living conditions maintain transmission.
  • Households may experience substantial treatment-related financial burden.
  • The national response includes molecular screening, portable imaging, shorter all-oral drug-resistant regimens, and routine BCG vaccination.

Constituents and virulence of tubercle bacilli

ConstituentRole in disease and immunity
Mycolic acids and other lipids
  • Responsible for acid-fastness.
  • Contribute to tissue damage.
  • Mycolic acid combined with muramyl peptide supports granuloma formation.
  • Released phospholipids induce caseous necrosis.
  • Waxy lipids create a delayed hypersensitivity response.
Cord factor
Trehalose 6,6-dimycolate
  • Produces tight serpentine rope-like cords.
  • Described as the most virulent property of tuberculosis in the lecture.
  • Inhibits white-cell migration.
  • Promotes chronic granuloma formation.
  • Acts as a powerful immune adjuvant.
Sulfatide
  • Prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion.
  • Allows intracellular survival and multiplication inside macrophages.
Surface proteins
  • Act as antigens.
  • Each mycobacterial species has proteins capable of producing a tuberculin response.
  • Purified protein derivative is used for the Mantoux skin test.
Cell-wall polysaccharides
  • Peptidoglycan provides structure.
  • Arabinogalactan links peptidoglycan to mycolic acid.
  • Lipoarabinomannan and lipomannan contribute to immune interaction.

Transmission and initial infection

1

Airborne release
Talking, coughing, or sneezing releases droplet nuclei.

2

Deep inhalation
Small particles bypass upper-airway turbulent clearance and reach alveoli.

3

Macrophage uptake
Alveolar macrophages phagocytose the bacilli.

4

Blocked killing
Sulfatide prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion.

5

Intracellular growth
Bacilli multiply in macrophages and create a localized infection.

6

Cell-mediated response
Th1 cells and activated macrophages form a granuloma after delayed immunity develops.

Transmission summary
  • Airborne droplet nuclei are expelled by coughing, sneezing, or talking.
  • Prolonged close contact is usually required.
  • Smear positivity and cavitary disease increase infectiousness.
  • M. bovis can be acquired through unpasteurized dairy products.

Two principal lesions

Exudative lesion

  • Acute inflammatory reaction.
  • Polymorphonuclear cells, leukocytes, and monocytes surround bacilli.
  • Resembles bacterial pneumonia early in the response.
  • Delayed hypersensitivity follows.
  • Macrophages, helper T cells, and multinucleated giant cells organize around infection.
  • Langhans giant cells have peripheral horseshoe-arranged nuclei.
  • PPD becomes positive.
  • Immunocompetent hosts may resolve the exudate.
  • Immunocompromised hosts may progress to necrosis and productive lesions.

Productive or proliferative lesion

  • Fully developed granuloma is called a tubercle.
  • Center contains giant cells and bacilli.
  • Middle zone contains pale epithelioid macrophages.
  • Periphery contains fibroblasts and lymphocytes.
  • Fibrous containment develops around the lesion.
  • Center undergoes cheese-like caseous necrosis.
  • Liquefaction and drainage into a bronchus produce a cavity.
  • Healing may occur through fibrosis and calcification.

Spread in the host

RouteMechanismResult
LymphaticBacilli move from the primary focus to regional lymph nodes.Lymphadenopathy and the hilar-node component of the Ghon complex.
HematogenousBacilli enter the bloodstream after leaving lymphatics or eroding a vein.
  • Miliary millet-seed distribution.
  • Kidney involvement with sterile pyuria.
  • Meningitis.
  • Pott disease.
  • Adrenal disease and Addison disease.
  • Hepatitis, scrofula, and mycobacterial arthritis.
BronchialCaseous material ruptures into a bronchus.Cough, airway spread, bronchopneumonia, and cavitation.
GastrointestinalInfected sputum is swallowed.Gastrointestinal seeding and intestinal tuberculosis.
Intracellular safe house
  • Bacilli reside in monocytes, reticuloendothelial cells, and giant cells.
  • Intracellular location makes chemotherapy difficult.
  • Drug penetration is reduced.
  • Persistence supports latent infection and later reactivation.

Primary versus secondary tuberculosis

FeaturePrimary tuberculosisSecondary or reactivation tuberculosis
TimingFirst exposure, commonly in childhood.Reactivation of dormant bacilli or less commonly reinfection.
Typical locationMid or lower lung zones, often subpleural.Posterior upper lobes and lung apices with high oxygen tension.
Clinical patternOften asymptomatic or mild in an immunocompetent host.More likely symptomatic, cavitary, infectious, and transmissible.
Characteristic lesion
  • Ghon focus is the peripheral parenchymal lesion.
  • Ghon focus plus hilar lymph node involvement forms the Ghon complex.
  • Fibrosis and calcification form the Ranke complex or calcified Ghon complex.
  • Rapid memory T-cell response produces caseous necrosis.
  • Fibrocaseous cavities may form.
  • Large cavities permit airway and lymphatic dissemination.
Failure of containmentChildren and immunocompromised patients may develop progressive primary TB.Occurs when cell-mediated immunity declines.

Clinical manifestations

Classic triadFever, night sweats, and weight loss.
Pulmonary tuberculosisExtrapulmonary tuberculosis
  • Productive cough lasting more than two to three weeks.
  • Hemoptysis or blood-streaked sputum.
  • Low-grade fever, often worse in the evening.
  • Drenching night sweats.
  • Unintentional weight loss.
  • Fatigue.
  • Chest pain and dyspnea in advanced disease.
  • Apical cavities in reactivation disease.
  • Lymphadenitis or scrofula with chronic painless neck swelling.
  • Pleural TB with exudative lymphocyte-predominant effusion.
  • Pott disease with thoracolumbar vertebral involvement and possible gibbus deformity.
  • CNS TB with basilar meningitis and lymphocytic pleocytosis.
  • Genitourinary TB with sterile pyuria.
  • Miliary TB from hematogenous dissemination.
  • Adrenal, hepatic, joint, and gastrointestinal disease.

Tuberculin skin test and IGRA

TST or PPD

  • Also called the Mantoux test.
  • Inject 5 tuberculin units in 0.1 mL intradermally on the volar forearm.
  • Previously sensitized T cells produce a delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
  • Read at 48 to 72 hours.
  • Measure induration, not redness.
  • A positive result supports infection but does not prove active disease.
  • False negatives may occur with overwhelming TB, HIV, Hodgkin disease, sarcoidosis, immunosuppressive drugs, or other severe immunosuppression.
  • The lecture warns that BCG may produce a false-positive reaction.

IGRA

  • Blood test that measures interferon-gamma release after exposure to TB-specific antigens.
  • Uses antigens such as ESAT-6 and CFP-10.
  • More specific for TB than a broad mycobacterial response.
  • Less affected by prior BCG vaccination.
  • QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus and T-SPOT are listed.
  • A positive result supports infection but does not prove active disease.
  • Does not directly detect organism DNA.
IndurationPositive in lecture forExamples
5 mmHigh-risk patientsHIV and recent close contact with active TB.
10 mmIncreased-risk groupsPeople from high-prevalence settings and intravenous-drug users.
15 mm or moreLow-risk patientsPeople without a major risk factor in the lecture table.

Proving active disease

1

Choose specimen
Fresh sputum, gastric washing, urine, pleural fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, joint fluid, biopsy, or blood according to site.

2

Process specimen
Liquefy with N-acetyl-L-cysteine and decontaminate nonsterile material with sodium hydroxide.

3

Smear
Use acid-fast staining or fluorescence microscopy for a rapid screen.

4

NAAT
GeneXpert or Truenat rapidly detects MTB and selected resistance markers.

5

Culture
Grow the organism in broth and solid media. Culture is the isolation standard and permits susceptibility testing.

6

Integrate imaging
Chest radiography or other imaging shows location and extent but does not replace microbiologic confirmation.

Test interpretation trap
  • TST and IGRA show immune sensitization.
  • They do not prove that active organisms are currently causing disease.
  • Isolation, molecular detection, smear, clinical findings, and imaging answer different questions.

Active-tuberculosis treatment

Core regimen
  • Initial phase uses rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
  • The lecture describes two months of RIPE followed by four months of rifampin and isoniazid.
  • Duration and regimen may change according to site, response, susceptibility, and protocol.
  • Using multiple drugs prevents selection of resistant organisms.
DrugMechanismMajor lecture adverse effects and reminders
RifampinInhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and blocks RNA synthesis.
  • Hepatotoxicity.
  • Red-orange discoloration of body fluids.
  • Important drug interactions.
  • Rifabutin may replace rifampin in the HIV context described in the lecture.
IsoniazidInhibits mycolic-acid synthesis.
  • Hepatotoxicity.
  • Peripheral neuropathy.
  • Give pyridoxine to patients at risk for neuropathy.
PyrazinamideWorks best in the acidic intracellular environment.
  • Hepatotoxicity.
  • Hyperuricemia.
EthambutolInhibits arabinogalactan synthesis in the cell wall.
  • Optic neuritis.
  • Red-green color-vision change.
  • Visual monitoring is important.
Directly observed therapy
  • The DOH uses directly observed therapy or DOT.
  • Medication may be provided through barangay-based programs.
  • Observation supports adherence, completion, prevention of relapse, reduced transmission, and prevention of resistance.

Drug resistance

ResistanceLecture-associated mutation
Isoniazid resistancekatG and inhA
Rifampin resistancerpoB
Fluoroquinolone resistancegyrA
  • MDR-TB and XDR-TB are major global problems.
  • The lecture defines XDR-TB as MDR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance and resistance to at least one additional key second-line agent.
  • Pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid are discussed for highly resistant disease.
  • Drug-resistant tuberculosis requires specialized susceptibility-guided regimens.

Latent infection

Regimen abbreviationLecture regimen
3HPIsoniazid plus rifapentine weekly for three months.
3HRIsoniazid plus rifampin daily for three months.
4RRifampin daily for four months.
6HIsoniazid daily for six months.
Latent versus active
  • Latent infection means positive immune testing, no symptoms, no active multiplication causing disease, and no contagiousness.
  • Active disease means symptoms or organ involvement, bacteriologic or clinical evidence, need for multidrug therapy, and possible transmission.

Prevention and control

LevelMeasures in the lecture
Administrative controls
  • Rapid identification of suspected or confirmed active TB.
  • Separate the patient.
  • Implement cough etiquette.
  • Screen healthcare workers.
  • Perform active case finding and contact tracing.
  • Use rapid molecular diagnostics.
Environmental controls
  • Adequate natural ventilation.
  • HEPA filtration where used.
  • Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation where used.
Personal protective equipment
  • N95 respirators for airborne protection.
  • Surgical masks for source control.
Vaccination
  • BCG is a live attenuated M. bovis vaccine.
  • Given to newborns in the Philippine immunization program.
  • Provides important protection against childhood TB meningitis and miliary TB.
  • Does not prevent every infection or all adult pulmonary disease.
Other prevention
  • Manage immunosuppression when possible.
  • Pasteurize milk to prevent M. bovis.
  • Reduce stigma.
  • Provide nutrition and living-condition support.
  • Educate communities and support treatment completion.

Nontuberculous mycobacteria

General NTM pattern
  • Environmental organisms in water, soil, and related reservoirs.
  • Usually not transmitted person to person.
  • Cause opportunistic disease in structural lung disease, HIV, immunosuppression, or device exposure.
  • May produce pulmonary, disseminated, lymph-node, skin, soft-tissue, or device disease.
Mycobacterium avium complex Mycobacteria pp. 7–9

Members and habitat

  • Includes M. avium, M. chimaera, and M. intracellulare.
  • The species cause a similar spectrum and are often grouped together.
  • Found in water, soil, birds, household plumbing, and aerosols.
  • Most common isolated NTM in the lecture.

Characteristics

  • Nonmotile.
  • Facultative intracellular.
  • Aerobic.
  • Slow growing.
  • High mycolic-acid content and acid-fast staining.
  • May grow optimally at warm temperatures and form smooth nonpigmented colonies.

Clinical patterns

  • Chronic pulmonary disease in older adults with bronchiectasis or structural lung disease.
  • Disseminated disease in advanced AIDS.
  • Risk is especially high with CD4 counts below 50 cells per microliter.
  • Lymphadenitis.
  • May involve organs outside the lungs.
  • Chronic indolent course and difficult eradication.

Treatment and prevention

  • Standard combination uses a macrolide, ethambutol, and a rifamycin.
  • Severe disease may include a limited course of intravenous aminoglycoside.
  • Refractory disease may use inhaled amikacin or clofazimine.
  • Pulmonary treatment continues for 12 months after negative sputum culture.
  • MAC lymphadenitis may be treated by surgical excision.
  • Macrolide prophylaxis is discussed for AIDS with CD4 below 50.
  • Reduce aerosolized water and soil exposure in vulnerable patients.

Other nontuberculous mycobacteria

OrganismDisease and differentiating clueLecture management
Mycobacterium kansasii
  • Second to MAC as a cause of NTM lung disease.
  • Tap water is a reservoir.
  • Photochromogen.
  • Slow grower at approximately 37°C.
  • Produces pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease resembling tuberculosis.
Isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol are listed.
Mycobacterium ulcerans
  • Causes Buruli ulcer.
  • Associated with tropical wetlands and aquatic insects.
  • Not transmitted person to person.
  • Prefers cooler temperature.
  • Begins as a painless subcutaneous nodule.
  • Progresses to necrotizing skin ulcer and severe edema.
The lecture describes an eight-week antimicrobial course.
Mycobacterium scrofulaceum
  • Environmental photochromogen.
  • Classic cause of chronic cervical lymphadenitis in children.
  • Often resistant to anti-TB drugs.
Surgical excision is emphasized.
Mycobacterium marinum
  • Fish-tank or swimming granuloma.
  • Appears two to three weeks after minor water-associated trauma.
  • Violet papule or nodule on fingers, toes, or elbows.
  • May ulcerate and spread along lymphatics in a sporotrichoid pattern.
  • Photochromogen that prefers 28°C to 30°C.
Rifampin plus ethambutol are listed.
Rapid growers
