  • Visible colonies in less than seven days.
  • M. fortuitum group occurs in soil and water and may resist TB drugs.
  • M. abscessus causes skin, soft-tissue, and difficult respiratory disease, including cystic-fibrosis disease.
  • M. chelonae is linked with postsurgical or post-traumatic skin and soft-tissue infection.
Species-specific susceptibility is required because resistance patterns vary.
Mycobacterium leprae and leprosy Mycobacteria pp. 9–12

Biology

  • Rod-shaped acid-fast bacillus.
  • Waxy hydrophobic cell wall with mycolic acid.
  • Visualized with Ziehl-Neelsen, Kinyoun, or fluorochrome methods.
  • Obligate intracellular organism.
  • Targets macrophages and Schwann cells.
  • Obligate aerobe.
  • Prefers cooler temperatures of approximately 27°C to 33°C.
  • Involves skin, superficial peripheral nerves, mucous membranes, face, and cooler extremities.
  • Cannot be routinely cultivated in vitro.
  • Can be propagated in armadillos or mouse footpads.

Transmission and risk

  • Prolonged close contact and respiratory droplets from untreated multibacillary patients.
  • Low infectivity and long incubation of approximately 2 to 10 years.
  • Most people have natural immunity.
  • Risk factors include close contact, armadillo exposure, older age, diabetes, malignancy, HIV, and other immunosuppression.
  • The disease remains associated with poverty, crowding, delayed diagnosis, stigma, and gaps in access.

Central pathogenesis

  • The type of cell-mediated immune response determines the spectrum.
  • Strong Th1 immunity limits bacillary multiplication.
  • Weak Th2-skewed cellular immunity permits widespread intracellular multiplication.
  • Nerve invasion produces sensory loss, weakness, deformity, and secondary injury.

Diagnosis

  • Clinical examination of skin sensation and peripheral nerves.
  • Skin biopsy with acid-fast staining.
  • Slit-skin smear.
  • PCR can directly detect bacterial DNA.
  • Lepromin test helps classify immune response rather than serving as the primary diagnostic test.

Tuberculoid versus lepromatous leprosy

FeatureTuberculoid formLepromatous form
Immune response
  • Strong Th1 cell-mediated response.
  • IL-2 activates cytotoxic T cells.
  • Interferon-gamma activates macrophages and natural-killer cells.
  • Weak cell-mediated and Th2-skewed response.
  • IL-4, IL-5, and IL-10 support antibody production.
  • Humoral response is ineffective against intracellular bacilli.
Bacillary load
  • Paucibacillary.
  • Few organisms in lesions.
  • Very few acid-fast bacilli on smear.
  • Multibacillary.
  • High bacterial load.
  • Many acid-fast bacilli and globi in lipid-laden foam cells.
Skin lesions
  • Few well-demarcated hypopigmented or reddish patches.
  • Anesthesia in lesions.
  • Asymmetric distribution.
  • Numerous raised poorly demarcated lesions.
  • Diffuse skin infiltration and nodules.
  • Symmetric distribution.
  • Leonine facies and loss of eyebrows or eyelashes.
Nerve involvement
  • Mild but asymmetric nerve enlargement.
  • May cause claw hand or foot drop in late disease.
  • Symmetric extensive nerve involvement.
  • Glove-and-stocking sensory loss.
  • Paresthesia, deformity, nasal collapse, and loss of digits may occur.
Other findingsGranulomas are prominent.
  • Chronic uveitis.
  • Facial-nerve paralysis and lagophthalmos.
  • Corneal drying and ulceration.
Lepromin testPositive.Negative.
Treatment durationRifampin and dapsone for six months in the lecture.Rifampin, dapsone, and clofazimine for 12 months in the lecture.

Prevention and public health

  • Early and accurate diagnosis.
  • Prompt multidrug therapy to stop progression and reduce spread.
  • Active case finding, household contact tracing, community surveys, and school-based screening.
  • Single-dose rifampin post-exposure prophylaxis for eligible contacts.
  • BCG offers cross-protection.
  • Prevent disability and provide rehabilitation.
  • Reduce stigma and discrimination.
  • Continue surveillance and monitoring through the National Leprosy Control Program.

If you see this cluster

Anesthetic skin patch + enlarged peripheral nerve is the central leprosy clue. Few sharply defined asymmetric lesions indicate tuberculoid disease. Numerous diffuse symmetric lesions with many bacilli indicate lepromatous disease.

5. Biofilm and device-associated disease

S. epidermidis

Prototype device biofilm: prosthetic valves/joints, shunts and catheters. coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive.

S. aureus

Can form biofilm on implants but also causes aggressive invasive and toxin-mediated disease.

P. aeruginosa

Slime layer creates a community resistant to phagocytosis and antibiotics. important in CF, burns and equipment.

A. baumannii

Biofilm + desiccation survival + resistance make it a persistent nosocomial pathogen on ventilators and surfaces.

Proteus

Catheter-associated urinary infection. urease and biofilm promote encrustation and stones.

Viridans streptococci

Dextran/glycocalyx supports dental plaque and adherence to previously damaged valves.

FindingThinkKey separator
Painless black eschar with surrounding edema/vesiclesCutaneous anthraxAnimal product/soil spore exposure. B. anthracis laboratory pattern
Necrotic skin lesion during Pseudomonas sepsisEcthyma gangrenosumBurn/immunocompromised/neonatal context. blue-green organism clues
Clean, hard, painless chancrePrimary syphilisLater generalized rash including palms/soles in secondary stage
Expanding erythema migransLyme diseaseIxodes exposure and later neurologic/cardiac/joint manifestations
Maculopapular/petechial rash with vector exposureRickettsial diseaseObligately intracellular endothelial infection. serology/PCR rather than routine culture
Hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with sensory lossLeprosyPeripheral nerve involvement. tuberculoid vs lepromatous spectrum
Lecture mnemonics worth protectingFaKSHet: Klebsiella and Shigella have no H antigen. K(e)SH P: Shigella and Proteus have no K antigen. MOPS: meningitis, otitis, pneumonia, sinusitis for pneumococcus. “Be serious”: B. cereus and fried rice. ABCDE(F)G: diphtheria toxin chain. ESKAPE: includes E. faecium, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, Enterobacter.
Final rapid review

Cram Sheet

This final tab is arranged as a sequence. Start with identification, move to the defining mechanism, then finish with the syndrome, emergency, diagnosis, and lecture prevention clue.

Final tab
Fast exam sequence
  1. Identify the stain and shape.
  2. Check the oxygen requirement.
  3. Use the single strongest laboratory discriminator.
  4. Match the exposure, host, or device.
  5. Connect the virulence factor or toxin to the syndrome.
  6. Choose the correct specimen and special test.
  7. Recognize the emergency and prevention step.

1. Identification branches

Starting findingNext testHigh-yield branch
Gram-positive cocci in clustersCatalase then coagulaseS. aureus is catalase positive and coagulase positive. Coagulase-negative species are separated by novobiocin.
Gram-positive cocci in pairs or chainsHemolysis, bacitracin, CAMP, optochinGAS is bacitracin sensitive. GBS is CAMP positive. Pneumococcus is optochin sensitive. Viridans is optochin resistant.
Gram-negative diplococciCarbohydrate useGonococcus uses glucose only. Meningococcus uses glucose and maltose and has a capsule.
Gram-positive rodsSpore, motility, shape, acid-fastnessAnthrax is nonmotile and spore-forming. Diphtheria has metachromatic granules. Listeria tumbles at 25°C. Nocardia is weakly acid-fast.
Gram-negative enteric rodsLactose, motility, H₂S, urease, indole, citrateE. coli is metallic green on EMB. Klebsiella is mucoid and nonmotile. Salmonella is motile and H₂S positive. Shigella is nonmotile and H₂S negative. Proteus swarms and is urease positive.
Gram-negative non-enteric rodsOxidase, pigment, temperature, special mediaPseudomonas is oxidase positive, grows at 42°C, and makes blue-green pigment. Haemophilus needs X and V. Legionella needs BCYE.
Thin corkscrew organismExposure and specialized visualizationSyphilis, relapsing fever, Lyme disease, or leptospirosis.
Acid-fast rodSmear, NAAT, culture, immune testThink tuberculosis, leprosy, or NTM. Mycolic acid explains acid-fastness and slow growth.

2. Aerobic cocci

Staphylococci

  • S. aureus means clusters, catalase positive, coagulase positive, golden colonies, abscesses, bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia, and toxin syndromes.
  • Protein A binds Fc of IgG.
  • TSST-1 causes fever, rash, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction.
  • Exfoliative toxin causes scalded-skin syndrome.
  • Heat-stable enterotoxin causes rapid vomiting and diarrhea without fever.
  • mecA or SCCmec produces altered PBP and MRSA.
  • S. epidermidis means biofilm and prosthetic devices. It is novobiocin sensitive.
  • S. saprophyticus means UTI in young women. It is novobiocin resistant.

Streptococci

  • GAS is beta hemolytic and bacitracin sensitive. Think pharyngitis, skin infection, scarlet fever, invasive disease, ARF after pharyngitis, and PSGN after throat or skin infection.
  • GBS is beta hemolytic, CAMP positive, and hippurate positive. Think maternal colonization and neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis.
  • Pneumococcus is an alpha-hemolytic lancet diplococcus that is optochin sensitive and bile soluble. Remember MOPS.
  • Viridans is alpha hemolytic and optochin resistant. Think dental caries and subacute endocarditis on damaged valves.

Neisseria

  • N. gonorrhoeae has no capsule, uses glucose only, attaches with pili, and causes urethritis, cervicitis, PID, neonatal ophthalmia, and disseminated arthritis-dermatitis.
  • N. meningitidis has a capsule, uses glucose and maltose, and causes meningitis or meningococcemia.
  • Petechiae, DIC, shock, and adrenal hemorrhage mean fulminant meningococcemia and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
  • Close contacts receive lecture-listed prophylaxis.

3. Gram-positive rods

Spore-formers

  • B. anthracis has a D-glutamate capsule on pXO2 and PA, EF, and LF toxins on pXO1.
  • Painless black eschar means cutaneous anthrax.
  • Hemorrhagic mediastinal disease after inhalation means Woolsorter disease.
  • Medusa-head colonies and gamma-phage lysis support the diagnosis.
  • B. cereus emetic disease occurs in 1 to 6 hours after fried rice. Diarrheal disease occurs in 6 to 24 hours after meat or sauce.

Diphtheria and Listeria

  • C. diphtheriae has club-shaped rods, Chinese-letter arrangement, and metachromatic granules.
  • Diphtheria toxin A subunit ADP-ribosylates EF-2 and stops protein synthesis.
  • Pseudomembrane, bull neck, airway obstruction, myocarditis, and paralysis are key clues.
  • Listeria is a cold-tolerant, tumbling, facultative intracellular rod.
  • Internalins enter the cell. Listeriolysin O escapes the vacuole. ActA uses host actin for cell-to-cell spread.
  • Think pregnancy, newborns, older adults, immunocompromise, unpasteurized dairy, deli meats, and soft cheese.

Branching rods

  • Nocardia is aerobic and weakly acid-fast. Think pulmonary or disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts and breadcrumb colonies.
  • Actinomyces is anaerobic, non-acid-fast, and associated with sulfur granules and chronic draining sinuses.
  • Streptomyces is an aerobic soil organism linked to antibiotic production and mycetoma.

4. Gram-negative enterics

OrganismBench clueMechanism and disease cue
E. coliPink MacConkey, metallic green EMB, IMViC positive positive negative negativeUPEC causes UTI. ETEC causes traveler’s watery diarrhea. EPEC causes infantile diarrhea. EHEC produces Shiga toxin and HUS. EIEC is invasive. EAEC forms aggregative biofilm and mucoid diarrhea.
SalmonellaMotile, non-lactose, H₂S positive, black centersM-cell invasion and macrophage survival. Nontyphoidal gastroenteritis versus typhoid with step-ladder fever, Faget sign, rose spots, and perforation risk.
ShigellaNonmotile, no H₂S, no gas, no H or K antigenIpa invasion, IcsA actin tail, dysentery, fever, tenesmus, low infectious dose, and possible HUS.
KlebsiellaLarge mucoid pink colonies, nonmotile, string testThick capsule, currant-jelly pneumonia, catheter UTI, liver abscess, ESBL, and CRE.
ProteusSwarming, strong urease, PAD positive, H₂S positiveAlkaline urine, struvite stones, staghorn calculus, catheter biofilm, and recurrent UTI.
CitrobacterVariable lactose and H₂S, citrate positiveOpportunistic UTI and sepsis. C. koseri is linked to neonatal meningitis and brain abscess.
HUS cueBloody diarrhea followed 5 to 10 days later by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure means HUS. The lecture warns against loperamide and antibiotic use in suspected EHEC or STEC.

5. Gram-negative non-enterics and curved rods

Nonfermenters

  • Pseudomonas means oxidase positive, 42°C growth, fruity odor, pyocyanin, pyoverdin, biofilm, burns, CF, swimmer’s ear, hot-tub folliculitis, green nail, and ecthyma gangrenosum.
  • B. cepacia means CF and contaminated hospital fluids.
  • B. pseudomallei means melioidosis, bipolar staining, and soil or water exposure.
  • A. baumannii means oxidase-negative coccobacillus, desiccation survival, biofilm, VAP, bloodstream infection, and MDR nosocomial disease.

Fastidious respiratory rods

  • H. influenzae needs X and V factors. Chocolate agar and satellitism support growth. Hib PRP capsule causes invasive disease.
  • B. pertussis progresses from catarrhal to paroxysmal to convalescent disease. Think whoop and post-tussive vomiting.
  • Legionella needs BCYE and comes from water aerosols. It survives in macrophages and causes atypical pneumonia.

Curved rods

  • C. jejuni is a gull-wing microaerophile that grows at 42°C. Think poultry, inflammatory diarrhea, and Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • H. pylori is urease positive and microaerophilic. Think gastritis, peptic ulcer, and gastric carcinoma risk.
  • V. cholerae causes rice-water stool and severe dehydration. TCBS is yellow.
  • V. parahaemolyticus means marine seafood and Kanagawa phenomenon.
  • V. vulnificus means raw oyster or seawater exposure with wound infection or septicemia, especially in liver disease.

6. Anaerobes

Recognition and collection

  • Think anaerobes with foul odor, abscess, necrosis, gas, mucosal-adjacent infection, bite wounds, black pigment, sulfur granules, or no growth in aerobic culture.
  • Anaerobic infections are commonly polymicrobial.
  • Collect deep aspirate, abscess material, blood, or normally sterile fluid.
  • Exclude oxygen and transport promptly.

Major organisms

  • B. fragilis is a bile-resistant colonic rod that promotes abscess formation. BBEA darkens with esculin hydrolysis.
  • Prevotella and Porphyromonas produce brown-black pigment and brick-red fluorescence.
  • Fusobacterium is fusiform and linked to oral infection. F. necrophorum is the exogenous species emphasized.
  • Actinomyces produces sulfur granules and draining sinuses.
  • Cutibacterium acnes is deep-skin flora linked to acne and device infection.

Clostridia

  • C. perfringens alpha toxin destroys membranes and causes gas gangrene or food poisoning.
  • C. tetani blocks inhibitory neurotransmission and causes spastic paralysis, trismus, and risus sardonicus.
  • C. botulinum blocks acetylcholine release and causes descending flaccid paralysis.
  • C. difficile follows antibiotic disruption of flora and causes pseudomembranous colitis.

7. Spirochetes and atypical bacteria

Spirochetes

  • T. pallidum means hard chancre, palms-and-soles rash, condyloma lata, latency, gummas, neurologic disease, and cardiovascular disease.
  • Screen and follow therapy with a nontreponemal test. Confirm with a treponemal test.
  • Penicillin is the lecture treatment of choice. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction occurs after rapid spirochete killing.
  • Borrelia relapsing fever uses antigenic variation and produces alternating febrile and afebrile periods.
  • Lyme disease means Ixodes exposure, erythema migrans, and later neurologic, cardiac, or joint disease.
  • Leptospira means animal urine or floodwater, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and renal involvement.

Wall-less and obligate intracellular organisms

  • Mycoplasma has no cell wall and contains membrane sterols. Beta-lactams do not target it.
  • M. pneumoniae causes walking pneumonia and extrapulmonary manifestations.
  • Chlamydia has an infectious elementary body and replicative reticulate body.
  • C. trachomatis causes ocular, genital, neonatal, and LGV disease.
  • Rickettsia infects endothelium and causes vasculitis and rash.
  • Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever after aerosolized animal exposure and does not require an arthropod vector in the lecture.
  • Anaplasma forms morulae in granulocytes. Ehrlichia forms morulae in monocytes.

8. Mycobacteria

Core identity

  • Acid-fast, aerobic, nonmotile, non-spore-forming rods.
  • Mycolic-acid-rich wall explains acid-fastness, resistance to drying, clumping, slow drug penetration, and slow culture.
  • Ziehl-Neelsen shows red bacilli on a blue background.
  • Fluorochrome stain shows yellow-orange fluorescence.
  • Culture media include Löwenstein-Jensen, Middlebrook agar, and MGIT broth.

Tuberculosis

  • Droplet nuclei reach alveoli and enter macrophages.
  • Sulfatide prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion.
  • Cell-mediated immunity forms granulomas with Langhans giant cells and caseation.
  • Liquefaction into a bronchus produces cavities.
  • Primary TB favors mid or lower lung zones in the lecture. Reactivation favors oxygen-rich apices.
  • Classic triad is fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
  • Active disease is treated with multidrug RIPE therapy in the lecture.

Testing and NTM

  • AFB smear detects bacilli but does not fully identify the species.
  • NAAT rapidly detects MTB and selected resistance markers.
  • Culture confirms and permits susceptibility testing.
  • TST and IGRA show immune sensitization, not automatically active disease.
  • MAC is the common NTM.
  • M. kansasii is photochromogenic and causes TB-like lung disease.
  • M. ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer.
  • M. leprae prefers cooler tissues and peripheral nerves.
  • Tuberculoid leprosy has strong cell-mediated immunity and few bacilli. Lepromatous leprosy has weak cell-mediated immunity and many bacilli.

9. Emergencies and do-not-miss warnings

Clinical clueThinkImmediate concern
Petechiae or purpura with meningitis and shockN. meningitidisDIC, hypovolemic shock, adrenal hemorrhage, and rapid death.
Bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, petechiae, and oliguriaSTEC or Shigella-associated HUSHemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure.
Gray pseudomembrane with bull neckDiphtheriaAirway obstruction, myocarditis, and paralysis. Antitoxin timing matters.
Rapid tissue necrosis with gasC. perfringensMyonecrosis, shock, and need for source control.
Trismus and generalized spasmsTetanusRespiratory and autonomic complications.
Descending flaccid weaknessBotulismRespiratory paralysis.
Profuse watery stool with severe dehydrationCholeraHypovolemic shock. Rehydration is the first priority.
Chronic cough with apical cavityActive pulmonary TBAirborne transmission and need for prolonged multidrug treatment.

10. Lecture mnemonics

MOPS

Meningitis, Otitis, Pneumonia, Sinusitis for pneumococcus.

Be serious

Think Bacillus cereus after fried rice.

FaKSHet

Klebsiella and Shigella have no H antigen.

K(e)SH P

Shigella and Proteus have no K antigen.

ABCDE(F)G

ADP-ribosylation, Beta prophage, Corynebacterium, Diphtheriae, Elongation factor, Granules.

ESKAPE

Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter.

Final exam habitWhen two organisms fit the syndrome, return to one decisive clue. Use coagulase, optochin, CAMP, maltose, sorbitol, H₂S, urease, oxidase, X and V factors, oxygen requirement, special medium, vector, food, water, animal exposure, pregnancy, device, or prior antibiotic use.
